## [Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17241) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Ballad introduces an online bandit algorithm that adaptively selects among a pool of LLMs during automated heuristic discovery, after empirically showing that larger, costlier models do not consistently yield better heuristics on NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems. Across five problems and four models, Ballad matches the best individual LLM in hindsight, sometimes surpasses every soloist, and reduces API cost by up to 65.6% compared to always using the strongest model. This work challenges the common assumption that bigger models are always better for code generation and heuristic design, and offers a cost-efficient orchestration method that could make automated heuristic discovery more accessible. It also introduces a novel bandit formulation for non-stationary, entangled reward signals, which may inspire further research in adaptive LLM selection. Ballad employs an LLM selection policy favoring rare, high-scoring heuristics over stable averages, a DAG-based credit propagation mechanism through the genealogy of the heuristic population, and discounting of stale observations to track each model's current utility. The approach addresses the non-stationarity and entanglement of rewards caused by one LLM's output seeding the context for subsequent calls.

## [CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17316) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CoReMem introduces a cost-internalizing framework for coding agents that selects memory for unknown future tasks by measuring its prospective value against write/read costs, using prospective segment valuation and actor adaptation. On ChainSWE, it raises a 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7% while using 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer cache-aware tokens. This work addresses a real bottleneck in agentic coding: deciding what to remember across successive tasks on an evolving repository without knowing the next task. By explicitly internalizing memory costs, it could lead to more efficient and scalable coding agents that maintain useful context without exploding token or compute budgets. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors (repository locations and executable checks). Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count, while provenance-gated value credit assigns additional value only to steps using memory-supplied anchors.

KernelMosaic introduces an open dataset pairing diverse CUDA tasks with verified solutions and trajectories, plus an agentic framework that guides a strong LLM through implementation, correctness repair, and performance optimization. Supervised fine-tuning of a small open-source model on this dataset raises correctness from 4%, 0%, and 0% to 88%, 82%, and 16% on KernelBench L1, L2, and L3, respectively. ## [Abstention Is Not Threshold Compliance: Stated Scoring Rules in Open Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14661) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper empirically tests whether language models comply with a stated probability threshold t for abstention, as proposed by Kalai et al., across 12 checkpoints from four open 3-8B model recipes. It finds that adding a simple abstention format line ('answer or I abstain') raises abstention rates from 20% to 91% at t=0.75, but varying t from 0.5 to 0.9 within that format changes abstention by only -0.8 percentage points, showing that abstention is driven by formatting rather than threshold compliance. This finding undermines a proposed calibration method for AI safety, showing that high abstention rates are not evidence of threshold compliance and that models may answer items they should abstain from. It affects evaluations that rely on stated scoring rules and suggests that safety-critical abstention behavior cannot be assumed from prompt instructions alone. Without the abstention format line, higher thresholds even lowered abstention, and up to 40% of a checkpoint's items received decisions that no compliant policy with threshold-independent beliefs could make. Comparisons with self-assessment signals like P(True) depended on the grader and on answer drift, and a post-hoc recalibrated P(True) threshold beat the abstention format at t=0.5 when calibrated on the evaluation distribution but fell below it at t=0.75 when calibrated on TriviaQA and applied to PopQA.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Kalai et al. proposed that a model should state a scoring rule in its prompt with an explicit threshold t, answering only when its probability of being correct exceeds t. This is a form of calibration, where a model's confidence should align with its actual accuracy, and abstention is meant to prevent incorrect answers when confidence is low. The paper tests whether open models actually follow this rule, probing compliance across multiple post-training stages and model sizes up to 32B.

## [Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14704) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes 'code explanations'—programs that explain LLM behavior across a dataset and can be automatically verified—and introduces a Consistency metric to evaluate and select candidate explanations. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, the authors find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings, and that these explanations are 6× to 100× shorter than chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations. This work addresses a key limitation of current LLM explanations like chain-of-thought, which are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. By making explanations executable and automatically verifiable, it offers a more scalable and objective way to understand and audit LLM behavior, which is important as LLMs make increasingly consequential decisions. The Consistency metric measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs. Results show that consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns; providing consistency feedback and code execution to Claude Opus 5.5 improves explanation consistency but it remains lower on complex tasks.

## [G2Image converts graphs into fixed-size image tensors for lightweight 2D encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14750) ⭐️ 7.0/10

G2Image introduces a fixed-budget graph imaging framework that converts each graph into two complementary image-like views: TopoGrid, which encodes an intrinsic bifiltration as a compact multipersistence surface grid, and GraphGrid, which aggregates edge densities between groups defined by intrinsic node scores. Both views are permutation-invariant and come with resolution-controlled stability guarantees, and they can be processed by lightweight 2D encoders aligned through a supervised cross-view contrastive objective. This addresses a fundamental challenge in graph learning: the lack of a standardized input interface comparable to patches in vision or tokens in language, which makes it difficult to reuse architectures across tasks. By enabling graphs to be processed by lightweight 2D encoders, G2Image could broaden the reuse of vision architectures for graph representation learning and simplify model design. The representations are fixed-size tensors, making them compatible with standard 2D encoders, and the framework extends to attribute-rich molecular graphs without changing the overall architecture. Across graph classification and molecular prediction benchmarks, G2Image achieves strong average performance, improves over single-view and standard fusion variants, and provides permutation invariance and stability guarantees.

**Background**: Graph learning deals with irregular data that varies in size and density and is invariant under node relabeling, making it hard to standardize inputs across tasks and architectures. Topological data analysis (TDA) provides tools like persistent homology and bifiltrations to capture multi-scale topological features, while multipersistence surfaces summarize two-parameter persistence compactly. ## [MDU: A Multilingual Document Understanding Benchmark for VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14758) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces MDU, a multilingual document-understanding benchmark comprising 23,146 examples across 13 tasks and five languages (English, French, German, Italian, Spanish), and evaluates 45 open-weight VLMs ranging from 1.7B to 235B parameters plus one commercial system. The benchmark is far from saturated: the best average score is 69.0, only eight systems reach 65, and the top two results come from 27B models rather than the largest ones. This benchmark exposes a non-saturated capability gap in multilingual document understanding, showing that scaling model size alone does not close language gaps or improve all capabilities uniformly. It provides the document-AI and VLM communities with a more comprehensive evaluation tool that covers diverse languages, tasks, and layouts, highlighting where current models fall short. The benchmark isolates complementary capabilities from surface-level text and Markdown extraction to summarization, classification, named-entity recognition, and layout-sensitive passage and layout extraction. Analysis shows that per-task scores are largely uncorrelated after controlling for overall model quality, and transcription ability specifically trades off against semantic extraction, while the gap between strongest and weakest languages persists even when controlling for domain composition.

## [Graph Label Alignment Diagnoses Benchmark Difficulty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14760) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces graph label alignment, a lightweight diagnostic that uses two supervised probes—structural label alignment (SLA) and feature label alignment (FLA)—computed without training a graph encoder to measure label accessibility in graph classification benchmarks. Across real benchmarks and multiple pooled backbones, the SLA–FLA plane strongly organizes test accuracy, with low-alignment datasets forming a regime where standard pooled pipelines struggle. This data-centric diagnostic helps distinguish whether benchmark success comes from genuine structure–feature reasoning or from label signal accessible via marginal views, which could influence benchmark design and model evaluation in graph learning. It offers a practical tool for assessing the difficulty and validity of graph classification tasks. SLA is based on permutation-invariant topological and spectral summaries, while FLA uses pooled node features with edges removed; the authors also introduce controlled interaction-dominated stress tests, including heterophilic ego-graphs and synthetic Twins tasks, to probe beyond marginal accessibility.

A new arXiv preprint (2611.14808) introduces OverServe, a multi-agent framework that co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts to trick LLM-based SaaS agents into repeatedly checking an unfinished condition, thereby extending execution and wasting provider resources. The attack works because each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt, and the tested tool specifications triggered no alerts in evaluated MCP scanners. ## [FairSumEval: Evidence-aware evaluation for discharge summaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14823) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces FairSumEval, an evidence-aware, fact-level evaluation framework for discharge summary generation that distinguishes facts supported by clinical notes from reference-only content. On 200 MIMIC-III admissions, it finds that 18.8% of physician reference facts have identified support in prior evidence, compared with 65.4% and 63.5% for facts generated by general-purpose and medically specialized models. Standard reference-based metrics conflate failure to recover available information with failure to reproduce content absent from the model input, which can mislead clinical NLP evaluation. FairSumEval separates these error types, offering a more faithful assessment of whether models are truly evidence-grounded, with practical implications for healthcare AI validation. The framework uses two complementary metrics, Soft IoU-S and Soft IoU-NS, to measure reference-generation agreement for facts with and without identified evidence support. Overlap is substantially higher for supported content (0.255 and 0.236) than for unsupported content (0.030 and 0.026), and the two scores are weakly correlated (rho = 0.22 and 0.17), showing conventional metrics do not consistently capture both dimensions.

The analysis shows that perturbations induce substantial shifts in deep semantic representations and that input gradients of different surrogate encoders exhibit directional alignment, suggesting shared adversarially sensitive directions underlie transferability.

## [World Models Lose Task-Relevant Information During Imagination, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14955) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A case study of a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) world model with active-inference planning in the CARLA driving simulator reveals a 'posterior-prior gap': posterior states retain obstacle information (AUC 0.85) while imagined prior states progressively lose it (AUC drops to 0.71 over 15 steps, logit separation down 57%). Because the same probe is used, the decay isolates the transition model as the bottleneck, and the planner's ensemble-based epistemic uncertainty fails to detect the loss (AUC 0.52, chance level). This finding exposes a critical failure mode in model-based planning: imagined rollouts can silently discard task-relevant signals, and the planner's own uncertainty estimates may not flag it, leading to unflagged imagination failures. It affects any system relying on world models for decision-making, such as autonomous driving and model-based reinforcement learning, and calls for direct measurement of information propagation in transition models. The study is a single-seed case study, limiting generalizability, and obstacle avoidance drops to 0% without privileged runtime coordinates. As a secondary contribution, task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components yields lane keeping (81.2±1.8% route completion) and obstacle avoidance (28/28 avoided, using privileged coordinates) in CARLA, with runtime weight modulation enabling post-evasion centering.

The paper shows that rank prizes in open frontier challenges are gameable when identities are free, as demonstrated by a replay where one solver's steps under two identities would have won first and second prize. It proposes a prediction-market rule that pays each accepted step for its added progress, which provably resists splitting and merging attacks and makes extra identities unprofitable. This work provides formal guidance for designing incentive mechanisms in machine-learning contests and prediction markets, addressing Sybil attacks and noisy score manipulation that can undermine fairness. It is valuable for organizers of open challenges who need robust payment rules. With noisy scores, the paper proves that any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something on average to a change that does nothing. It proposes a submission fee at least equal to what luck pays per attempt, but notes that nothing enforces the noise bound and the rule does not cap total payments under noise.

## [Nullasar: Generative Model Learns Quasar Variability Beyond DRW](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15040) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Nullasar, a generative model trained with flow matching that learns quasar optical variability directly from time-series data without assuming a parametric noise model. It demonstrates that Nullasar can generate light curves that deviate from the Gaussian damped random walk (DRW) model and, when used as a null hypothesis for periodic signal detection, performs comparably to fitting the correct DRW model and outperforms parametric fitting when variability follows a more flexible AR(2) process. The DRW model is widely used as a null hypothesis in time-domain astronomy, but its incompleteness can bias significance estimates for periodic signals (e.g., from supermassive black hole binaries) and extreme variability events like tidal disruption events (TDEs) and changing-look quasars. Nullasar offers a data-driven alternative that could improve the reliability of such detections, impacting upcoming surveys like LSST that will produce massive quasar light curves. Nullasar is trained with flow matching and can learn correlated distributions of noise parameters, generating light curves from a range of deviations from the Gaussian DRW. A practical limitation is sensitivity to contamination of the training set by non-null signals, which the authors mitigate by projecting the conditioning vector onto its leading principal components.

## [Binary Tokenization Is NP-Hard to Approximate, Paper Proves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15074) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.15074) proves that the Binary Tokenization problem—selecting at most K substrings to minimize the total token count for a binary corpus—has no polynomial-time n^{1-ε}-approximation algorithm for any fixed ε∈(0,1) unless P=NP. It also presents a polynomial-time (γ,γ)-bicriteria approximation algorithm with γ = √M log n, where M is the maximum document length, and an (O(log n log B), O(log n log B))-bicriteria algorithm for a storage-budget variant. Tokenization is a fundamental preprocessing step for modern large language models, and this result shows that finding an optimal vocabulary is computationally intractable even to approximate within a polynomial factor. The bicriteria algorithm offers a provable trade-off, giving theoretical grounding for heuristic tokenizer design and highlighting the inherent difficulty of the problem. The hardness holds for every fixed ε∈(0,1), meaning no polynomial-time algorithm can approximate the optimal token count within a factor of n^{1-ε} unless P=NP. The bicriteria algorithm may use up to γK vocabulary entries and produce up to γ·OPT_K tokens, where OPT_K is the optimum under budget K; the storage-budget variant bounds the sum of selected substring lengths by B and achieves an (O(log n log B), O(log n log B)) approximation for 2≤B<n.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Tokenization is the process of splitting text into smaller units (tokens) that a language model can process; common methods like Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) build a vocabulary of subword units to balance compression and expressiveness. The Binary Tokenization problem abstracts this as selecting a set of substrings from a binary corpus to minimize the total number of tokens needed to represent all documents, with each document segmented separately. In complexity theory, NP-hardness of approximation means that even finding an approximate solution is computationally intractable unless P=NP, and a bicriteria approximation algorithm allows a bounded violation of one constraint (e.g., vocabulary size) while guaranteeing a bound on the objective (token count).

Implemented in SGLang with about 80 lines of code, it achieves 3.7x speedup on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x on an RTX A6000 compared to stock SGLang with FlashInfer. This addresses a real memory-bandwidth bottleneck in document QA, data labeling, and LLM-based evaluation workloads, where many questions share the same long context. The approach is practical and easy to adopt, potentially improving throughput significantly for these common tasks. The method uses a stream-id attention mask evaluated inside the attention kernel to keep each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question, without needing a dense tensor. Every decode step has a fixed shape captured as a CUDA graph, and it was faster than stock SGLang in all 144 timed runs across two GPUs, two releases, six workloads, and six input sets.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: LLM inference typically involves a prefill stage that computes the KV cache for the input prompt, followed by a decode stage that generates tokens one by one. Prefix caching avoids recomputing the KV cache for shared prefixes, but during decoding, each question still reads the entire document's KV cache separately, making decoding memory-bandwidth bound. SGLang is a high-performance serving framework for large language models that supports such optimizations.

## [Learned Constraint Selection Fails to Beat Fixed Umbrella Set in SCOPF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15142) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A systematic study evaluates learned constraint selection for security-constrained optimal power flow (SCOPF) against a fixed umbrella set that enforces all constraints observed to bind in training. Across all PGLib-OPF networks up to 10,000 buses, the umbrella set is never outperformed, with a median size of only five constraints, while the learned selector gains at most 0.25 ms and violates constraints on 4-5% of instances. This negative result challenges the prevailing assumption that learned constraint selection is necessary for speed-ups in SCOPF, with practical implications for the learning-to-optimize community. It suggests that simpler learning-free baselines may suffice for fixed-network SCOPF, potentially redirecting research efforts toward settings where learning truly pays, such as unit commitment. The paper introduces the criterion 'price of a spare' to determine when learning can pay: an enforced but inactive constraint is free, so the umbrella is exactly optimal wherever feasible, and learning can only help where a spare decision carries a price. In unit commitment, a static commitment loses 4-12% out of sample, but a predict-repair-reduce pipeline recovers it with a cost gap of 0.2-2.9%, full feasibility, and 16-161x speed-up over the MILP.

**Background**: Security-constrained optimal power flow (SCOPF) is a fundamental optimization problem in power systems that ensures the grid operates reliably even after contingencies like line outages. ## [FréchetFlow: Flow Matching for Non-Euclidean Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15220) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FréchetFlow introduces a flow matching framework for metric space-valued data that learns Euclidean flows on distances to landmarks and reconstructs objects via weighted Fréchet means, avoiding the need for manifold structure. The paper establishes Wasserstein error bounds and proves consistency under finite second moments, with convergence rates depending on metric complexity, tail moments, and fitting accuracy. This work extends generative modeling to general metric spaces where manifold structures are unavailable, enabling principled generation for scientific data such as probability distributions, trees, and covariance matrices. It provides theoretical guarantees that connect generation accuracy to landmark placement and reconstruction error, which could impact researchers in generative models and non-Euclidean data analysis. The method requires neither linear operations nor a smooth manifold structure, and it leverages well-established Euclidean flows to learn the joint distribution of landmark distances. Experiments show competitive accuracy with established flow matching methods in Euclidean simulations and lower Wasserstein errors than tailored methods on several scientific datasets, with generation error decreasing as sample size increases.

**Background**: Flow matching is a simulation-free generative modeling framework that trains continuous normalizing flows by learning a vector field that morphs a simple reference distribution into complex data. The Fréchet mean generalizes the notion of a centroid to metric spaces, providing a natural way to compute averages of points when only distances are defined. Wasserstein distance measures the discrepancy between probability distributions and is commonly used to bound the error of generative models.

## [Breath-Dx: A Benchmark for eNose-Based Disease Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15348) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Under realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance; recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance, while demographic confounders (e.g., age) matter for some conditions.

## [LGPO Eliminates Importance Sampling Ratios for Stable LLM Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15404) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper proposes Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO), which replaces ratio-based importance sampling with likelihood-based gating to enforce a soft trust region constraint, eliminating the need to compute old-policy likelihoods. Experiments show LGPO achieves comparable stability and peak performance to GRPO while reducing training time by ~18% on average, and remains stable in fully on-policy settings where GRPO fails. This work challenges the necessity of importance sampling ratios in LLM reinforcement learning, potentially simplifying the training pipeline and reducing computational overhead for post-training large language models. If adopted, it could make RL-based fine-tuning more efficient and robust across different training regimes, benefiting practitioners who rely on methods like GRPO. The paper demonstrates that removing the importance sampling correction term does not harm training stability, whereas removing the trust region mechanism can lead to collapse. It also highlights that ratio-based clipping can fail in fully on-policy training because the importance ratio stays at 1, so the trust region constraint never activates.

## [TRACE Audits Audio-Language Models for Inconsistent Evidence Ordering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15463) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TRACE introduces a source-level counterfactual auditing method that deletes the queried sound and each rival in turn, checking whether every view containing the target outscores the view without it. Across 8 large audio-language models and 3,456 controlled mixtures, 6.3% of correct answers fail this ordering test, and a simpler target-only score check misses 42.5% of these failures. This reveals a subtle but important failure mode: models can answer correctly without consistently ordering evidence, meaning accuracy alone does not certify genuine source discrimination. The finding affects evaluation and interpretability practices for audio-language models and highlights the need for counterfactual auditing in safety-critical deployments. The failure rate rises from 4.9% to 8.4% as target SNR falls from +5 dB to -5 dB, even on units correct at every level, and the effect survives loudness and re-pairing controls. The conflict cannot be repaired by any shared threshold, and code and data are available on GitHub.

**Background**: Large audio-language models (LALMs) combine high-capacity audio encoders with large language models to understand and reason about speech, music, and environmental sounds. Counterfactual auditing tests a model's behavior by systematically removing or altering inputs to see if its internal evidence ranking changes consistently. TRACE extends this idea to the source level, asking whether a model ranks views containing a target sound above views where it is absent.

## [Rule-Based Oracle Detects Silent Information Loss in LLM API Translations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15543) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces isloss, a deterministic oracle that maps source and translated LLM API requests and replies to a shared intermediate representation called ConvIR and applies explicit rules to detect silent information loss. In evaluations, isloss detected 95/125 planted faults (76.0%) with only 2/100 false alarms (2.0%), and found that 18.5% of completed translations passed static checks while silently altering prompt, role, or tool information. As LLM applications increasingly rely on translators and compatibility layers to move conversations across APIs, silent loss of instruction roles, tool interactions, or generation controls can corrupt agent execution and model evaluation. This work establishes conversation preservation as a distinct correctness requirement for reliable LLM interoperability. Unlike schema validation or reference-based differential testing, isloss requires neither a reference translation nor additional model calls, and it distinguishes avoidable loss from degradation caused by target API limitations. In translated replies, 203/558 streams (36.4%) caused exceptions or silent corruption in at least one tested official OpenAI SDK, and targeted experiments across six models showed that translation-induced changes can alter model behavior.

## [TraceKV: Policy-Preserving Low-Rank KV Cache Compression for Reasoning VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15569) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TraceKV introduces a training-free low-rank KV cache compression framework that unifies on-policy calibration, sensitivity-aware SVD, and global rank allocation to preserve the reasoning policy of vision-language models. It achieves near-lossless reasoning accuracy with 5.64× KV cache compression when combined with quantization, and up to 1.83× end-to-end decoding speedup with optimized low-rank attention kernels. Reasoning VLMs face substantial KV cache demands from large multimodal contexts and growing reasoning traces, making efficient inference a critical bottleneck. TraceKV's policy-preserving approach addresses reasoning failures caused by policy drift in existing low-rank methods, enabling practical deployment of reasoning VLMs with significantly reduced memory and faster decoding. The method identifies two causes of degradation: calibration-state mismatch between static contexts and on-policy reasoning states, and unequal error sensitivity across KV states. It substantially reduces policy-KL divergence during reasoning, and code will be available at https://github.com/AK-DREAM/TraceKV.

**Background**: KV cache stores key-value states of previous tokens to avoid recomputation during autoregressive generation, but its memory footprint grows with context length and reasoning traces. Low-rank compression reduces this by storing low-dimensional latents of KV states, and can be combined with quantization for further savings. However, existing low-rank methods often cause the compressed model's predictive distribution to drift from the dense model, leading to reasoning failures. TraceKV addresses this by calibrating on on-policy reasoning states and allocating ranks based on sensitivity.

## [Do Scaling Laws Hold for Universal Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15603) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This arXiv paper empirically tests whether neural scaling laws apply to machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) by training M3GNet, MACE, and PET on subsets of a combined MatPES-MP-ALOE dataset ranging from 10,000 to 1.16 million structures, while comparing uniform random sampling against chemistry-informed stratification, iterative DIRECT, and embedding-based furthest-point sampling. The authors find power-law improvements with more data, but the scaling exponent, error floor, and relative sample efficiency vary by model architecture, target quantity, sampling policy, and test-set distribution. For AI-driven materials science, this work shows that simply adding more first-principles calculations is not enough—the chemical and configurational content of new data must align with the model's intended use, which directly affects how practitioners budget expensive DFT data generation. It also cautions that sampling-policy rankings can reverse across test distributions, meaning benchmark results may not transfer to real-world deployment. Chemical stratification improved cross-dataset performance on the distribution-shifted MP-r²SCAN test set but degraded in-distribution performance, while embedding-space diversity policies frequently underperformed plain random sampling. The authors also report that relative loss is strongly associated with test-to-train chemical-space divergence, underscoring that structure count is a necessary but insufficient scaling variable.

**Background**: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are data-driven surrogate models that predict energies, forces, and material properties with near quantum accuracy at a fraction of the cost of first-principles methods like DFT. A new arXiv paper (2611.15621) demonstrates that random matrix theory (RMT)-based data-free metrics for neural networks are not invariant under functionally preserving reparameterisations, meaning they can take arbitrary values without changing the model's function. The authors exploit the phenomenon of criticality—where some layers are 'robust' and can be re-initialized without affecting output—to construct such reparameterisations across multiple architectures and scales. This finding undermines the use of RMT-based metrics for pre-training optimization and post-training compression, as these metrics are shown to be unrelated to model performance or generalization. It challenges a popular interpretability approach and urges the community to reconsider data-free layer-wise analysis methods. The paper shows that relationships between RMT metrics are spuriously related to generalization, and that whether many pre-trained models have metrics in a 'good' range depends partly on model initialization. The results hold across a range of architectures and scales, with a project page available at https://gmw99.github.io/data-free-metrics-dont-work.

Functionally preserving reparameterisations are transformations that leave the network's input-output mapping unchanged, such as reinitializing certain layers. ## [Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation Estimates Peaks from Solution Contours](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15641) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces contour-assisted evolutionary computation, which treats evaluated solutions as spot heights and draws contour lines to identify and estimate peaks. It proposes a contour-assisted EA (CA-EA) and a surrogate-assisted version (CA-SAEA), showing significant evaluation reductions on 2-D benchmarks and competitive performance on the CEC 2015 expensive suite. This approach offers a novel way to leverage the spatial structure of evaluated solutions, potentially reducing the number of expensive evaluations needed in optimization. In 2-D, a contour tree with persistence separates significant peaks from interpolation ripples, while in higher dimensions hill climbing on the interpolated surface locates peaks and ray-cast level sets describe them. An area-law extrapolation estimates peak location, height, and shape, and CA-EA reduces evaluations by factors of 12 to 112 compared to a plain GA on 2-D benchmarks.

## [Mechanistic Framework Maps Where Uncertainty Is Observed in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15735) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a mechanistic framework that categorizes uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for large language models (LLMs) based on where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation, using four lenses: structural (component updates), representational (hidden states), distributional (token probabilities), and semantical (distributions over meanings). It relates these lenses through the residual stream and orders them by information content, providing a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. This framework bridges mechanistic interpretability and uncertainty quantification, offering a principled taxonomy that could guide the design of more reliable UQ methods and improve trustworthiness of LLM outputs. It affects researchers and practitioners working on safe deployment of LLMs, as it clarifies which observation points yield sufficient information for estimating specific uncertainty targets. The four lenses are ordered by the information they carry: structural lens observes component updates, representational lens observes hidden states, distributional lens observes token probabilities, and semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. The paper also distinguishes evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify UQ evaluation protocols, and identifies open problems connecting uncertainty estimation to internal computation and downstream use.

**Background**: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) helps LLMs recognize when their responses may be unreliable, which is critical for safe use. ## [HyLI: Model-Based RL for Parameterized Action Spaces via Latent Imagination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15744) ⭐️ 7.0/10

HyLI introduces a model-based agent that learns a hybrid policy entirely in the latent imagination of a world model and acts with a single forward pass, adding counterfactual mode evaluation and success-window replay to handle PAMDP-specific learning issues. On seven PAMDP benchmarks, it matches or exceeds the strongest model-free baseline within one standard deviation, reaches 90% of that score with 2.4x fewer environment steps (5.0x counting reward-free pre-training), and decides 67x faster than the model-based planner DLPA. This work bridges the gap between sample efficiency and real-time control in parameterized action reinforcement learning, showing that a model-based agent can be both more sample-efficient than model-free baselines and fast enough for real-time applications. It could impact robotics and other domains where actions have discrete modes with continuous parameters and quick decisions are required. HyLI's counterfactual mode evaluation provides a learning signal for every discrete action at every imagined state, while success-window replay retains rare successful experiences in training. The method is compared against DLPA, a model-based planner, and achieves a 67x faster decision speed at DLPA's published planner settings.

**Background**: Parameterized-action Markov decision processes (PAMDPs) require an agent to select a discrete action along with continuous parameters whose meaning depends on that action, such as choosing to move to a location with specific coordinates. Model-free methods learn directly from interactions but are sample-inefficient, while model-based methods learn a world model and plan, offering better sample efficiency but slower decision-making. Latent imagination, popularized by Dreamer, trains policies inside the compact latent space of a learned world model, enabling efficient learning without generating full observations.

## [Honesty Is a Race: Predicting When Verifiable-Reward RL Teaches a Model to Bluff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15779) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper derives a first-order condition for when reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) makes a model more honest, showing that honesty depends on a race between the checker's acceptance rate and the pull of unverifiable correct verdicts. Specifically, a GRPO step increases honesty exactly when p̃·r/b > 1+κ, where p̃ is the weighted checker acceptance rate, r is the reward for a verifiable certificate, b is the reward for an unverifiable verdict, and κ is the pull of items where the unverifiable verdict is correct. This work provides a precise theoretical condition for when RLVR leads to honest versus bluffing behavior, which is crucial for AI safety and the design of reward functions in RLHF. It helps practitioners predict and avoid reward hacking, where models learn to game the reward signal instead of solving the task. The analysis reveals that near the threshold, honesty is a race that a run just below the threshold can win, while a run under a lottery (random pay with the same mean) cannot. Additionally, the term κ starts large and falls, causing a run just above the threshold to first dip toward bluffing before recovering, and there is a ceiling on the payoff ratio above which the model gives the honest verdict even when it is wrong.

## [VibePrevisBench: New Benchmark Evaluates Coding Agents on 4D Scene Generation in Blender](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15789) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VibePrevisBench is a new 242-task benchmark that evaluates coding agents on reconstructing executable 4D scenes in Blender from briefs and rendering proxy videos. It scores each delivery via a rule-based Scene Check that re-runs code and compares the exported scene against hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions, plus a VLM-based Screen Check that asks a VLM judge whether passing facts are recognizable in the rendered video. This benchmark addresses a genuine gap in evaluating coding agents on long, multi-shot 4D reconstruction tasks, combining rule-based and VLM-based evaluation to assess both the underlying scene and its rendered output. Its analysis of 11 frontier agents provides insights for both agentic AI and graphics research, highlighting that multimodal understanding of space and camera motion separates agent performance. The benchmark spans four input kinds—scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos—and reveals three key observations: multimodal understanding separates agents (especially in space and camera motion), all agents master basic camera work and staging but fail at challenging requests, and agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct errors. These findings suggest agents need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

HeriKGQA is a new knowledge-graph question-answering method that confines the LLM to interpreting questions and phrasing answers, delegating all computation to SPARQL queries and deterministic code. On 500 questions over real sensor data from five cultural heritage sites, it achieves 99.0% accuracy, 18.2 points above the strongest of three baselines using the same LLM, while running almost four times faster. The system parses questions into intents constrained by a heritage ontology that aligns W3C SOSA/SSN with CIDOC-CRM, compiles them into SPARQL, and derives temporal, spatial, and anomaly facts through a grounding layer with error correction guarding each LLM step. Ablation shows that without grounding, accuracy drops by 12.2 points overall and from 99% to 66% on anomaly questions.

DuoJEPA trains separate self-supervised encoders per modality with the LeJEPA objective and adds a single transformer layer to translate between their embedding spaces, supervised by a contrastive loss in the target space. Experiments on chest radiographs/reports and Sentinel-2/Sentinel-1 imagery show strong cross-modal retrieval and classification without directly aligning the encoders' own spaces. This work challenges the common assumption that cross-modal learning requires aligning embedding spaces, showing that translation layers can enable retrieval and classification while keeping modality-specific spaces unaligned. It could lead to more flexible multimodal architectures and offers insight into how residual connections affect where cross-modal pressure is absorbed. The translator's residual connections determine whether alignment emerges: with a residual translator the encoders become directly aligned, while a skipless translator yields no detectable alignment but comparable cross-modal performance. The learned class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation of the source space, and on Sentinel data the translator retrieves the paired image among 4,000 candidates in 77-79% of cases.

## [Fit-LRP fits linear relaxations to non-convex polytopes for neural network verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16003) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Fit-LRP is a framework that exactly optimizes affine bounds over non-convex polyhedral domains by solving a sequence of small linear programs, enhancing the final optimization step of LiRPA and α,β-CROWN branch-and-bound. On ARCH-COMP and neural Lyapunov benchmarks, it reduces branching by 47×, cuts worst-case verification time by 15×, and verifies 6.1× faster than α,β-CROWN on a single CPU versus a GPU. State-of-the-art verifiers rely on axis-aligned box relaxations, which become extremely loose for oblique or non-convex regions common in cyber-physical systems, causing combinatorial blowup and non-termination. Fit-LRP eliminates box-induced over-approximations, enabling earlier pruning and making formal verification of neural network controllers more practical for safety-critical applications. The method represents non-convex domains as unions of polytopes and solves small, low-dimensional linear programs to exactly optimize the final affine bound of a nonlinear function over the exact polyhedral state-space constraints. It seamlessly integrates into the final optimization step of LiRPA and α,β-CROWN BaB, and with region-wise partitioning achieves significant speedups even on a single CPU.

**Background**: Neural network verification aims to prove that a network's output satisfies certain properties for all inputs in a given domain. The model uses a single backbone that simultaneously denoises, reasons about, and understands both the image and its depth, enabling three tasks: generating images with depth, estimating depth from photos, and painting images onto a given depth map. A new arXiv paper (2611.16065) designs and empirically compares two Solidity smart-contract reward systems for federated learning: one with public quality scores and one with ZK-proof-based privacy. Testing on MNIST with Sybil, zero-gradient, and noise attacks across three seeds, it finds that the privacy-preserving variant doubles adversary reward capture and introduces severe outcome variance. This exposes a fundamental tradeoff between cryptographic privacy and incentive fairness in blockchain-based federated learning, showing that static threshold ZK gates can fail as fairness mechanisms under realistic convergence dynamics. The findings are critical for designers of FL incentive layers who must balance privacy guarantees against robustness to adversarial participants. The vulnerability stems from a structural self-inclusion bias in cosine-similarity scoring: as the global model converges, legitimate gradient updates diminish and become statistically indistinguishable from bounded noise, letting adversaries breach the ZK threshold and trigger a late-stage failure cascade. The paper also provides a closed-form theorem formalizing the privacy–Sybil resistance tradeoff and maps mainnet deployment boundaries via linear gas scaling models, including the post-Fusaka EIP-7825 per-transaction gas cap.

It matters for AI safety and multi-agent systems research because it shows that suppressing communication can sacrifice utility, so safety interventions must be carefully balanced. The protocol scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets, and exploratory analyses show the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution. The authors caution that these effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates.

ORCHID-SAGE proposes encoding expert knowledge in formal protocols to automate CALPHAD assessments, enabling fully reproducible database construction from evidence to phase diagram. In a first demonstration on the Cr-Ni system, the database was regenerated with identical predictions by a script on a second machine, by an AI agent using only the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and by a refit from public sources alone. This work addresses a critical reproducibility gap in CALPHAD assessments, where expert judgment is rarely recorded, making databases impossible to regenerate or update. By enabling AI agents to update databases as new evidence arrives while keeping human judgment on record, it could accelerate materials design in self-driving laboratories and improve trust in thermodynamic databases. The approach is demonstrated only on the Cr-Ni binary system as a first attempt, and the protocol organizes the assessment record into reproducible and automatable steps. The database is no longer fixed at publication but can be updated by AI agents as self-driving laboratories and other sources provide new evidence, while human judgment remains on the record.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) is a computational method introduced in 1970 for modeling phase stability and thermodynamic properties of multicomponent materials, producing phase diagrams that show stable phases under different temperature and composition conditions. Building a CALPHAD database requires expert judgment at many steps, and because these decisions are rarely recorded, others can use a database but cannot regenerate or update it. Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can help build initial models from data, but the assessment itself—the sequence of judgments that turns data into a reliable database—is still carried out by human experts. Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate materials discovery, and predicting synthesis conditions is a key capability for them.

## [Shared Item-Level Error Limits Small Language Model Aggregation in Fermi Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16315) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A large-scale study analyzing 2.51 million answers from 15 open-weight language models (3B-72B parameters) on Fermi estimation tasks finds that shared item-level error dominates, so aggregating 30 models reduces error by only a median 1.7% (at most 5.4%) instead of the 74-79% expected from independent unbiased draws. This finding challenges the common averaging argument used to motivate multi-agent LLM systems, showing that simply adding more agents may yield diminishing returns when errors are correlated at the item level; it has direct implications for researchers and practitioners designing LLM ensembles and multi-agent architectures. The study decomposes log10 error into a model-item mean component and a residual, finding the item-level component accounts for a median 0.906 of error variance; three rounds of debate reduce within-team dispersion by 93% but leave the item-level component unchanged, and higher sampling temperature or activation steering have negligible effects.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Fermi estimation involves making rough order-of-magnitude estimates for quantities that are difficult to measure directly, often using back-of-the-envelope calculations. Multi-agent LLM systems often assume that aggregating independent unbiased estimates reduces error proportionally to 1/sqrt(N), but this study tests that assumption empirically using realFP, Science Olympiad Fermi questions, and a guesstimation set.

## [WIS-MeZO: Wanda-Guided Sparse Perturbations Boost Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16317) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose WIS-MeZO, a zeroth-order optimization method that uses Wanda weight-activation saliency to construct task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks while keeping the pretrained model dense. Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models (3B–32B parameters), WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. This work addresses a key bottleneck in memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning by showing that informative coordinate selection can substantially improve zeroth-order optimization. It could make forward-only fine-tuning more practical for large models where backpropagation memory is prohibitive. The method analyzes support quality via gradient energy capture and relates it to gradient estimation and convergence, with comparisons against random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations confirming the importance of informative support selection. The approach keeps the pretrained model dense, meaning sparsity is only in the perturbation masks, not in the model weights.

**Background**: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models by using only forward passes to estimate gradients, avoiding backpropagation and its memory overhead. MeZO is a prominent ZO optimizer that perturbs all parameters randomly, but high-dimensional random perturbations can be inefficient. Wanda is a post-training pruning method that scores weights by the product of weight magnitude and input activation norm, identifying important weights in a data-dependent way. Sparse perturbations reduce the search dimension, but selecting which coordinates to perturb is critical for performance.

## [Recursive SALM uses persistent latent state to adapt frozen GPT-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16375) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework where a persistent latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a pretrained language model. In experiments with a frozen GPT-2 small, latent-gated LoRA achieved 89.1% accuracy on a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, comparable to 88.0% for a full-context LoRA baseline, using only a 64-dimensional state to carry earlier evidence. This work suggests a path to extending language model context beyond finite token windows by compressing interaction history into a compact latent state, potentially enabling long-context reasoning without retraining the base model. If validated on larger models, it could impact how conversational agents and sequential decision-making systems handle memory. The experiments only evaluate the deterministic SALM formulation with a frozen GPT-2 small and exclude earlier evidence from the decoder context; zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. In a two-turn task with unseen codewords, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance but rarely generate the exact codeword under the evaluated training schedule.

**Background**: Language models typically rely on a finite token context window, which limits their ability to refer to earlier interactions. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that injects small trainable matrices into a pretrained model, and latent-gated LoRA extends this by using a latent state to gate the adaptation. ## [CoMem: Query-Guided Selective Context Compression via Contrastive Memory Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16384) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query, using Contrastive Compressor Learning and a same-context hard negative mining strategy. Experiments show CoMem consistently outperforms existing compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. This work addresses a key challenge in long-context LLM inference: task-relevant evidence varies across queries, so indiscriminate compression can lose critical information. CoMem's query-sensitive approach could enable more efficient and accurate inference on long documents, benefiting applications like retrieval-augmented generation and document question answering. CoMem introduces bidirectional attention among memory slots to overcome the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, and uses a same-context hard negative mining strategy that pairs a single document with multiple queries to force the compressor to retain query-specific evidence. The code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.

**Background**: Soft context compression converts long inputs into compact memory slots (soft tokens) to reduce inference cost for large language models. Contrastive learning trains models to distinguish similar and dissimilar examples, and hard negative mining selects challenging negative examples to improve discrimination. Query-guided compression tailors the compressed representation to the specific information needs of a given query, rather than compressing uniformly.

## [RESYNC synchronizes stale latent states to meet streaming deadlines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16523) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RESYNC proposes running a large model asynchronously while a fast latent-state updater synchronizes its stale representations with recent observations, allowing deadline-bound streaming inference to preserve much of the teacher's accuracy. Across one real and two synthetic streams and five architecture families, it beats the best compact or distilled alternative in all twelve dataset-architecture pairs, and in live replay with 1 ms arrivals it serves at least 99.4% of arrivals within the interval at 0.35–0.62 ms median latency on one CPU thread. This decouples a large model's accuracy from its latency, enabling real-time ML systems with strict per-observation deadlines to benefit from large-model quality without paying synchronous inference costs. It is relevant to streaming applications such as audio, video, and sensor processing where background compute is available but responses must be immediate. The updater learns from the frozen model's representations without task labels, and the share of the teacher's gain preserved is complete on the real stream but lower and generally declining with anchor age on synthetic streams. In live replay, RESYNC is around the same speed as or faster than the compact model and 7.9–17.7× faster than synchronous large-model inference.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Streaming inference requires a model to produce a prediction for each observation before the next one arrives, so a large accurate model may miss the deadline. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student to mimic a larger teacher, but compact models often sacrifice accuracy. RESYNC instead keeps the large model running asynchronously and uses a lightweight updater to refresh its stale latent state with recent observations, targeting settings with background compute available but a strict per-observation response deadline.

## [Dataset Distillation via Drifting in Latent Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16642) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new dataset distillation method called 'Drifting' learns synthetic samples by moving them in a feature extractor's latent space toward real data and away from each other, without using a classification objective. The method directly approximates per-class data distributions and is shown to cover the real distribution better than existing methods while still producing effective training samples. This work advances dataset distillation by offering a novel synthesis method that avoids classifier-dependent optimization, potentially improving data-efficient learning and enabling better visualization and interpretation of models. It also extends beyond images to other modalities, broadening the impact across machine learning applications. The method drifts distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor, moving samples toward real data and away from each other without a classification loss. The authors also propose distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation and demonstrate the approach as a visualization tool for model interpretation.

## [MobileProbe: Adaptive Red-Teaming for Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16693) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MobileProbe introduces a trajectory-aware red-teaming framework that adaptively evaluates mobile GUI agents against environmental injection attacks (EIAs) by discovering attacker-controllable content surfaces, localizing vulnerable decision points along the agent's trajectory, and iteratively refining context-aware payloads via a surrogate-filtered evolutionary loop. The authors construct a benchmark of 83 long-horizon attack instances across 12 mobile applications, each annotated with a Confidentiality, Integrity, or Availability (CIA) attack goal, and show higher attack success rates than human-written, zero-shot LLM, and prior automated red-teaming baselines on three representative agent architectures. Fixed-point benchmarks that pin hand-crafted payloads to a specific step of a specific task can underestimate the security risk of deployed mobile agents, because agents may take different routes and never reach the injected page. MobileProbe's adaptive, trajectory-aware approach improves test coverage and can serve as a pre-deployment auditing tool to systematically uncover vulnerabilities and inform security hardening of mobile agents. The benchmark comprises 83 long-horizon attack instances spanning 12 mobile applications, each annotated with a CIA attack goal to cover principal threat categories. MobileProbe outperforms human-written, zero-shot LLM, and prior automated red-teaming baselines adapted to the mobile domain, though as an arXiv preprint it has not yet undergone peer review.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Mobile GUI agents are AI systems that read a phone's screen and operate apps on a user's behalf to complete multi-step tasks such as online shopping or messaging. Because they act on whatever the screen shows, attackers can embed malicious instructions into ordinary UI content—an environmental injection attack (EIA)—to redirect the agent's actions. Red-teaming is the practice of adversarially testing systems to find security flaws before deployment, and trajectory-aware methods focus on the sequence of steps an agent takes rather than a single fixed point.

Most music foundation models rely on Transformers, whose quadratic attention complexity causes substantial compute and memory overhead for long recordings; MusicRWKV offers a promising architectural alternative that could enable more efficient long-sequence modeling in audio and music AI. If validated, this approach could lower the cost of training and deploying music understanding systems for researchers and practitioners working with full-length songs. The invertible compression module reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability, and FiLM conditioning provides modality-aware representation learning without cross-attention. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, and layer-wise telemetry reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper layers; however, the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

The paper introduces a Triplet Incremental Training Framework that adds 3D geometric awareness to general vision-language models (VLMs) for autonomous driving using automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, while preserving open-world capabilities. The framework employs a tri-stream pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM, an auxiliary depth stream for geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM with KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. It also challenges the assumption that heavy 3D priors are necessary, showing that off-the-shelf VLMs are highly adaptable. The auxiliary depth branch is discarded at deployment, ensuring zero inference overhead, and the method is evaluated on four benchmarks covering 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. It outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific experts in 3D perception, and retains original general reasoning capabilities.

## [Codebook Search Enables Multi-bit LLM Watermarking on Short Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16890) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes a codebook-based multi-bit watermarking scheme that maps an n-bit payload to a longer u-bit codeword and embeds it via token-level logit biasing, then recovers the payload by nearest-codeword search using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. Experiments show near-perfect recovery for 16–24 bit payloads on 200-token generations and strong performance on 127-token generations for base models. This work addresses a key limitation of existing multi-bit watermarking methods, which often require long generations or costly decoding, by enabling reliable payload recovery from short texts. It could improve attribution of short LLM-generated content, benefiting AI security and provenance tracking. The method struggles on some instruction-tuned models with very short texts due to low-entropy output distributions, and a BCH-based variant avoids codebook storage but generally reduces robustness. The Levenshtein variant improves resilience to deletions and light paraphrasing, while insertions and stronger rewrites remain challenging.

**Background**: Multi-bit LLM watermarking embeds a binary payload into generated text so it can later be extracted to identify the source model or user. Existing methods often require long generations or expensive decoding to recover the payload reliably. Codebook-based approaches map the payload to a longer codeword with error-correcting redundancy, and extraction finds the nearest codeword. BCH codes are a class of cyclic error-correcting codes that allow precise control over the number of correctable errors, and Levenshtein distance measures the minimum number of insertions, deletions, or substitutions needed to transform one string into another.

## [STEALTH: Robust Linguistic Steganography Survives Hardware and Precision Differences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16928) ⭐️ 7.0/10

STEALTH introduces a linguistic steganography scheme that remains decodable despite bit-level differences in token probabilities caused by varying floating-point precision, quantization, or GPU architecture. It uses an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise and a rateless spinal code decoded by beam search, achieving robust decoding across model families and hardware. This work addresses a fundamental fragility in provably secure linguistic steganography, which typically assumes bit-exact probability recomputation. By tolerating hardware and precision variations, STEALTH enables practical covert communication and has implications for watermarking and security of language model outputs. STEALTH decodes every message across all tested precisions, quantization levels, smaller models, and a different GPU architecture, and even across model families with separate vocabularies and tokenizers. It carries more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and both trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.

**Background**: Linguistic steganography hides secret messages within text generated by language models, aiming for stegotexts indistinguishable from normal samples without the key. Most provably secure schemes require the receiver to recompute the sender's token probabilities exactly, which is fragile to floating-point and hardware differences. Rateless spinal codes are a class of codes that adapt to channel conditions without fixed rate, and exponential race is a method for sampling from a distribution using pseudorandom noise.

## [SALA aligns latent actions via language for dual-axis scaling of embodied models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17110) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SALA introduces semantically aligned latent actions that use language descriptions of unpaired human and robot video clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence, without requiring paired data. This shared latent action space enables dual-axis scaling: pre-training on more general human video reduces robot action prediction error, and post-training on more task-specific human video improves real-world robot task success rates. This addresses a key challenge in embodied AI: aligning human and robot actions to leverage abundant egocentric human videos for robot policy learning. By enabling scaling along both pre-training and post-training axes, SALA could significantly reduce the cost of collecting robot interaction data and improve the generalization of embodied foundation models. SALA translates semantic similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. Unlike world-action models (WAMs), latent action models (LAMs) like SALA avoid explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution, offering greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs.

## [User Adaptivity Makes Offline LLM Benchmarks and Live A/B Tests Measure Different Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17239) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper formalizes how user adaptivity and prompt endogeneity cause offline benchmark evaluation and live A/B testing to target different causal quantities: the common-distribution effect and the induced-distribution effect, respectively. It defines these two estimands, shows that standard difference-in-means estimators converge to each, and characterizes when the two can rank models differently. This distinction can lead to different model rankings and deployment recommendations, so practitioners designing benchmarks or A/B tests need to be aware that offline results may not reproduce live decisions. It provides a theoretical basis for measuring both model performance and the user behavior changes the model induces. The paper gives a sufficient condition under which the two rankings are guaranteed to agree, offering a practical heuristic for judging whether offline evaluation suffices. It also shows in a stylized linear interaction model that user adaptivity can increase estimation variance, and argues that adaptivity is a common mechanism behind challenges like reward hacking and novelty effects.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: In interactive LLM systems, users adapt their prompts and task choices after seeing model responses, so the prompts a model is evaluated on depend on the model itself—a form of prompt endogeneity. Offline benchmarks use a fixed prompt set, while live A/B tests observe prompts generated through user interaction, and causal inference distinguishes estimands (the quantities being estimated) such as common-distribution versus induced-distribution effects. The difference-in-means estimator, which compares average outcomes between treatment and control groups, is the standard tool in both settings.

Crucially, the analysis shows that while context length is associated with this degradation, the number of instances has a stronger effect on final results. This is an important technical insight for practitioners who deploy LLMs on batch tasks such as aggregating sentiment across many reviews or analyzing multiple documents in a single prompt, since it warns that scaling up the number of instances can silently break accuracy. It also suggests that optimization efforts should focus on instance count, not just context length, when designing prompts and evaluation pipelines. The study evaluates tasks in which LLMs excel individually, and the degradation pattern is consistent across all tested models: a gradual decline for small instance counts (approximately 20–100) followed by a sharp collapse at larger counts. The paper is an arXiv preprint (v3) and has no community discussion yet, so its findings have not been peer-reviewed or widely debated.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Multi-instance processing (MIP) refers to feeding multiple inputs—such as several movie reviews or documents—into a single prompt and asking the LLM to analyze each one and aggregate the results. Prior work has shown that LLM performance often degrades as input context length grows, a phenomenon sometimes called "context rot," but little research had examined how the number of distinct instances, independent of raw token length, affects performance. This paper separates those two factors to identify which one drives the collapse.

## [MonitorBench: New Benchmark Evaluates Chain-of-Thought Monitorability in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28590) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers have introduced MonitorBench, a fully open-source benchmark for systematically evaluating the monitorability of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models. It includes 1,540 test instances across 19 tasks in 7 categories, each with carefully designed decision-critical factors, plus two prompting stress-test settings to quantify how much CoT monitorability can be degraded. CoT monitorability is increasingly seen as a fragile but valuable safety mechanism for overseeing advanced AI systems, so a standardized benchmark fills a critical gap in AI safety and interpretability research. MonitorBench enables systematic comparison of models and monitoring setups, supporting work on AI control, reasoning faithfulness, and stress-testing monitorability. Experiments show that CoT monitorability is a conditional property affected by the evaluated LLM, the monitor LLM, and task characteristics, and is higher when decision-critical factors shape intermediate reasoning rather than merely influencing the final answer. Under stress-test prompting, most evaluated LLMs can intentionally reduce monitorability, mainly on tasks where decision-critical factors are not structurally required by the reasoning process.

**Background**: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting encourages large language models to generate intermediate reasoning steps before producing a final answer, which can improve accuracy and make the model's reasoning more transparent. CoT monitorability refers to the ability to reliably detect latent misbehavior or misaligned intentions by inspecting these intermediate steps, serving as a potential safety control. However, CoTs are not always causally responsible for final outputs, and monitorability may be fragile and degrade under certain training or prompting conditions.

## [Submodular Coverage Objectives Improve Benchmark Selection for LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02209) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.02209v2) proposes using submodular coverage objectives—explained variance and facility location—to select a small set of benchmarks that best predict performance on all others, reducing LLM evaluation cost. On eleven score matrices from public evaluation results, these coverage objectives outperform traditional information-based objectives (entropy, mutual information) in predicting held-out model scores. This work addresses the costly and growing problem of evaluating LLMs on an ever-expanding collection of benchmarks by showing that a few well-chosen benchmarks can predict the rest. It could significantly reduce evaluation costs for researchers and practitioners, and the facility location objective offers practical benefits like classical guarantees and readable selections. The coverage objectives predict held-out model scores best where correlations can be estimated, and facility location performs practically as well as explained variance while providing classical guarantees (even under a budget) and readable selections. Information objectives fall behind because entropy favors benchmarks that the selection predicts poorly, and mutual information favors benchmarks that others predict well, not benchmarks that predict others.

**Background**: Submodular optimization deals with set functions that exhibit diminishing returns, making them suitable for tasks like feature selection and sensor placement. In LLM evaluation, scores across benchmarks are strongly correlated and concentrate in a few dimensions, so a few well-chosen benchmarks can largely determine the rest. Sensor placement methods, which select observations carrying the most information (measured by entropy or mutual information), provide a natural framework for choosing which benchmarks to run.

## [Optimal Screening Under Aleatoric Uncertainty for AI Resource Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07979) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper analyzes a two-stage resource allocation framework combining algorithmic targeting with physical screening, proving that the optimal strategy screens units at the margin of algorithmic allocation while directly targeting highest-risk units. The paper also shows that efficiency gains from screening grow with aleatoric uncertainty and derives a simple budget-splitting rule based only on the cost ratio. This work provides a theoretical foundation for designing hybrid allocation programs that mix AI predictions with human verification, which is relevant for social protection and humanitarian operations where misallocation is costly. It offers policymakers a principled way to decide how much budget to spend on screening versus direct allocation. The framework assumes a fixed coverage budget and irreducible aleatoric uncertainty over individual vulnerability status, meaning even perfect knowledge of conditional probabilities cannot eliminate misallocation. The optimal cutoff for splitting budget between screening and direct allocation depends only on their cost ratio, and the paper illustrates the approach with income-based social protection and humanitarian demining in Colombia.

## [Random Embedding Injection Matches Optimized Soft Prompts on Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11936) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.11936v3) introduces Random Soft Prompts (RSPs), which append a freshly sampled sequence of random embedding vectors—drawn from an isotropic Gaussian fitted to the pretrained embedding table—to LLM inputs without any training. RSPs achieve accuracy comparable to optimized soft prompts on math reasoning benchmarks in several settings, and the authors show the effect also transfers to DAPO training. This finding suggests that the benefit of soft prompts may come largely from the act of injecting extra positions rather than from learned content, which could simplify prompt engineering and reduce training costs for reasoning tasks. It also offers a unified lens for understanding various soft prompt methods that differ in training and form. The mechanism is two-stage: the random position flattens the distribution over the first few generated tokens, causing reasoning trajectories to branch, and then this influence dilutes as generation continues, allowing the response to commit to a single completion. Combined with temperature sampling, RSPs widen Pass@N, the probability that at least one of N attempts is correct.

This paper isolates the simplest form of soft prompt—training-free and freshly resampled—to test whether the gain comes from the learned content or from the injection itself. The random vectors are sampled from an isotropic Gaussian fitted to the entrywise mean and variance of the pretrained embedding table, ensuring they are statistically similar to real embeddings.

AutoScientists introduces a decentralized team of AI agents that self-organize around promising hypotheses, critique proposals before using compute, and share successes and failures to reduce redundant exploration.
