It could accelerate discovery in biomedical ML, model training, and protein engineering by making autonomous experimentation more efficient and robust under fixed budgets. The decentralized design allows agents to interpret a shared experimental state and self-organize without a central planner, preserving knowledge of failed directions to avoid redundant work. Evaluations span BioML-Bench (biomedical imaging, protein engineering, single-cell omics, drug discovery), GPT training optimization, and ProteinGym, all under matched experimental budgets.

POIROT introduces a modular protocol where agents in an LLM multi-agent system cast private votes within a hazard space derived from the system architecture, aggregating them into a single failure attribution. The protocol is built in phases—independent self-assessment, sharing assessments, and peer interrogation—and is evaluated on the Who&When benchmark and a new BLAME benchmark for clinical rehabilitation and algorithmic trading. Failure attribution is a key barrier to deploying LLM multi-agent systems in safety-critical domains, and POIROT removes the need for a centralized human or LLM judge that must hold the entire interaction history. The finding that independent self-assessment drives the benefit—while interaction can harm it—offers a counterintuitive design principle for reliable multi-agent oversight. Agent-based attribution outperforms a single-LLM evaluator in all nine model-benchmark configurations (up to +50 percentage points) only when sharing and interrogation are omitted; sharing makes agents converge on the same often-wrong culprit, and interrogation does not recover the loss. The study evaluates one proprietary and two open-weight LLMs, and both POIROT and BLAME are released as open source.

## [World-Model Collapse as a Phase Transition in Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31399) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2606.31399v3) empirically demonstrates that long-horizon language agents exhibit a phase-transition-like collapse in world-state tracking as task stress parameters cross a critical boundary. Through a large grid search over state size, state dependency, horizon, number of actions, observation mode, and state-change frequency, the authors map a phase diagram with low-stress success, a narrow critical region of sharp drop, and high-stress failure. This work frames world-model collapse as a measurable bottleneck for long-horizon agents, with implications for agent evaluation and reliability. It suggests that small changes in task parameters can cause sudden failure, so robustness testing must probe near critical boundaries rather than relying on average performance. Step-by-step traces reveal the mechanism: the agent loses track of the true world state before its actions become invalid, meaning it acts from a corrupted world model rather than merely choosing a bad action. ## [Audit reveals learned uncertainty in distributional RL often untrustworthy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11607) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper audits whether learned return distributions in distributional reinforcement learning can be trusted for risk-sensitive decisions by comparing them to environment-grounded distributions using statistical tests. Across QR-DQN, C51, and IQN on MinAtar (33 runs), 40-95% of the strongest claimed risk trade-offs are refuted at 95% confidence, and almost none can be confirmed. This work challenges the assumption that distributional RL methods provide reliable uncertainty estimates for risk-sensitive applications, showing that acting on learned CVaR advice can be worse than chance. It suggests that uncertainty estimates, including those from learned world models, should be validated against realized outcomes at decision points, impacting researchers and practitioners relying on such methods for trustworthy AI. The audit uses excess Wasserstein gap between top two actions (equal to violation mass of first-order stochastic dominance) to screen claims, then tests with permutation nulls, bootstrap refutation, and FDR control. Positive controls confirm 96-100% of real claims (correlation 0.89-0.92), and ensembling, risk-sensitive training, and recalibration do not fix the problem, with recalibration indicating learned spread has no usable information about true risk.

It achieves within ~10% error on Llama 3.1 and Mixtral 8x22B, and 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs, discovering a Mixtral configuration with +27% throughput over a published reference in under 30 minutes of single-node exploration. Configuring distributed training across hundreds of GPUs is a combinatorial nightmare where teams burn GPU-hours on trial and error; this tool replaces that with fast, accurate simulation, potentially saving significant cost and enabling pre-silicon planning. It matters for any team training large LLMs at scale, from research labs to industry practitioners. The projection engine uses GPU microbenchmarks on as few as one device to capture compute kernels and in-scope communication, while a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule; a pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU. The tuning agent combines a deterministic seed planner with an LLM investigation loop and an analytic memory pre-filter to reject infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent.

## [CauProphet: LLM agents build persistent causal cognition like humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32477) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce CauProphet, an LLM agent that maintains a persistent 'Causal Cognition' store and constructs a structured 'Causal Belief' for each task by combining prior causal knowledge with current evidence. The agent continuously updates both the belief and its long-term causal knowledge as new observations arrive, and in financial research it achieves a 25.4% improvement in mean rank correlation with next-day returns over a baseline agent, while raising prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Most LLM agents rely on retrieving past records or summaries, which limits them to episodic recall rather than genuine understanding of cause and effect. CauProphet's persistent causal knowledge and demonstrated transfer to downstream decision-making point toward next-generation agents that can accumulate reusable causal experience across tasks, which could benefit long-horizon domains such as finance, scientific research, and everyday planning. The approach is inspired by human causal cognition and separates a long-term Causal Cognition store from a task-specific Causal Belief that captures causal factors and the effects of possible actions. Evaluations cover financial research, scientific tasks, and everyday action selection, though the abstract is truncated and the reported gains come from the authors' own benchmarks, so independent replication is still needed.

## [Survey and Empirical Audit of Early Stopping in Large Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00166) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents a survey and empirical audit of early-stopping methods for large reasoning models, introducing a metric called Target-Integrated Token Efficiency (TITE) to measure efficiency relative to an oracle across accuracy targets. The study evaluates five reasoning models on math, science, code generation, and factuality tasks using a shared rollout replay protocol, and finds that correctness can degrade at later exit positions beyond what a fitted decoding-noise model predicts. Early stopping can significantly reduce inference costs for large reasoning models, which often generate unnecessarily long reasoning traces, so a rigorous audit of these methods helps practitioners choose reliable stopping strategies. The finding that later exits can hurt correctness and that reasoning may continue after forced termination highlights reliability risks that must be addressed before deployment. The audit uses a shared rollout replay protocol to compare methods fairly, and TITE measures efficiency relative to an oracle across accuracy targets. Reliability checks reveal continued reasoning after forced termination and weaker supporting reasoning in some correct early-stopping outputs, and the implementation is available on GitHub.

## [Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Model with Simplified Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03233) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Axion 1.0 is a fully open agent foundation model trained with only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage uses model-aware data construction to build self-contained reasoning, while the second stage extends to tool-dependent reasoning via a scalable pipeline for automatically verifiable tasks. This work shows that strong agentic capabilities can be achieved with a simple, reproducible recipe, challenging the trend of increasingly complex training pipelines. By releasing the complete recipe—including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code—Axion 1.0 lowers the barrier for researchers and developers to build and extend open agent models. The model-aware data construction synthesizes challenging problems and adversarially strengthens them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second SFT stage uses a scalable pipeline grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation to create diverse, automatically verifiable tasks, and reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and tool interaction.

AGORA is a new item-response-theory aggregator that learns judge reliability without human labels and outperforms Dawid-Skene on small evaluation sets. It models each item on a latent quality scale and each judge with a sensitivity parameter and ordered rating thresholds, jointly learning from all items. This addresses a practical problem in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, where human-labeled validation sets are often small (a few hundred items) and judge pools mix reliable and unreliable judges. Across three benchmarks, AGORA matches or exceeds Dawid-Skene on large sets, and its advantage widens as the set shrinks toward a few hundred items. It remains accurate as judge pools grow more uneven, and a label-free dispersion statistic indicates when trust weighting helps; code is available on GitHub.

## [SafeOrchestrate: Runtime-Checked LLM Orchestration for Cyber-Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09364) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SafeOrchestrate introduces a reference architecture that converts natural language intents into runtime-checkable LTL-style specifications for safely orchestrating cyber-physical systems via LLMs. In a Web of Things instantiation, it grounds specifications to Thing Description affordances exposed through MCP and verifies candidate actions against SMT-backed guardrails, achieving 100% required action accuracy and up to 100% MCP Execution Similarity versus a baseline that drops to 13% on complex tasks. This work addresses a critical safety gap in using LLMs to control physical systems, where unconstrained tool use can violate device capabilities and safety constraints. The architecture derives atomic goals from NL intents, generates LTL-style specifications, grounds them to TD affordances via MCP, and checks actions against SMT-backed guardrails. Evaluation on simulated smart home, greenhouse, and industrial automation tasks shows 100% required action accuracy and 100% MCP ES on all but one task (92%), while the direct LLM-to-MCP baseline degrades to 13% MCP ES on multi-device, event-triggered, and ordered tasks.

## [DForkTree fixes fork-induced accuracy collapse in block diffusion draft trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12356) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DForkTree introduces a training-free method that re-anchors each branch of a draft tree on its own tokens, correcting the drafter's top-1 accuracy drop from 89% to 18% after a fork. On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, it outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, achieving up to 41.5% improvement over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree, with average speedups of up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding. This work identifies and fixes a specific failure mode in block diffusion drafters, enabling more efficient speculative decoding without additional training. It could lead to immediate practical gains in LLM inference acceleration, benefiting deployment of large language models where latency matters. DForkTree adjusts the drafter's scores using pointwise mutual information from target-generated n-grams, weighted more heavily after a fork, and employs a layer-wise GPU search to recover the exact optimal tree under these scores. The method is training-free and shows that errors stem from conditioning on an outdated prefix rather than limited model capacity.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a lightweight drafter propose multiple tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, preserving output quality. Block diffusion drafters like DFlash predict an entire block of tokens in one forward pass, and DDTree builds draft trees from their per-position distributions to explore multiple branches. However, each distribution implicitly assumes the drafter's greedy continuation is accepted, causing accuracy to collapse when branches diverge from the greedy path.

## [Interpolation-Based Attack Breaches FedAvg Federated Learning Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06822) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces an interpolation-based approximation method that generates intermediate model updates, making data reconstruction attacks feasible in horizontal Federated Averaging (FedAvg) scenarios where clients share parameters only after multiple local steps. It also designs a layer-wise weighted loss function, with weights tuned by Bayesian optimization, to improve reconstruction quality, and experiments show the proposed AWA method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on image data reconstruction metrics. FedAvg is the most widely used federated learning algorithm, and this work demonstrates that it is vulnerable to data reconstruction attacks, undermining the privacy-preserving assumption of federated learning. This could significantly impact FL security research and motivate the development of stronger defenses for real-world deployments. The attack works by interpolating between model updates to approximate intermediate local training states, and the layer-wise weighted loss assigns different importance to updates from different neural network layers, with weights optimized via Bayesian optimization. The source code is publicly available on GitHub, and the method is evaluated on image data reconstruction tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Federated learning is a distributed machine learning paradigm where multiple clients collaboratively train a model without sharing their raw data, typically by exchanging model parameters or gradients. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) is the most common algorithm, where clients perform multiple local training steps and then share their model updates for aggregation. Data reconstruction attacks aim to recover clients' private training data from the shared parameters, and prior methods have mainly succeeded in settings where updates are shared after every local step, not in the FedAvg scenario.

The MDI compares per-token attention between text and non-text inputs, while the AEI normalizes each modality's attention share by its token share; the token compression method is simple and effectively rebalances attention, as shown by the dramatic MDI reduction on LLaVA-7B. FoMEMO introduces a decomposition-based training paradigm that converts multi-objective optimization into preference-wise aggregated posterior learning tasks, enabling scalable pre-training on hundreds of millions of synthetic datasets. At test time, the foundation model performs in-context posterior prediction and optimizes derived acquisition functions for efficient candidate generation without any model updates. This approach addresses the sample-efficiency challenge in expensive multi-objective optimization by amortizing optimization knowledge into a pre-trained foundation model, potentially reducing the need for costly real-world evaluations. It could benefit applications where each function evaluation is expensive, such as engineering design and drug discovery. The model is pre-trained on synthetic datasets without relying on extensive real-world domain experiments, and at inference it performs in-context learning to generalize to unseen problems and user preferences. ## [VMonarch: Structured Attention for Efficient Video Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22275) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VMonarch introduces a structured attention mechanism using Monarch matrices to enable sub-quadratic attention in Video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). It adapts spatio-temporal Monarch factorization, adds a recomputation strategy for stability, and proposes an online entropy algorithm fused into FlashAttention, reducing attention FLOPs by 17.5x and achieving over 5x speedup for long videos. The quadratic complexity of attention is a major bottleneck for scaling Video DiTs to longer videos and higher resolutions. VMonarch's approach could significantly reduce computational costs while maintaining generation quality, making high-quality video generation more accessible and enabling longer video synthesis. VMonarch achieves comparable or superior generation quality to full attention on VBench after minimal tuning, and surpasses state-of-the-art sparse attention methods at 90% sparsity. The code is available on GitHub, and the method includes specific techniques like spatio-temporal factorization and online entropy for fast Monarch matrix updates.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are transformer-based generative models that replace 3D U-Net architectures with latent token transformers, using 3D VAE encoding for video synthesis. Monarch matrices are a class of structured matrices that are hardware-efficient and expressive, parameterized as products of two block-diagonal matrices, enabling sub-quadratic attention via alternating minimization. FlashAttention is a fast and memory-efficient attention algorithm. VBench is a benchmark for video generation quality.

## [Transformers Learn Arithmetic via Shattered Compositionality, Not Human-Like Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22510) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2601.22510v3) shows that transformers trained on synthetic arithmetic tasks acquire skills in reverse order or in parallel rather than through human-like sequential rules, a phenomenon the authors call 'shattered compositionality'. The study provides evidence that correlational matching to training data, not causal or procedural composition, drives these learning dynamics. This work challenges assumptions about compositional learning in transformers and has implications for reasoning reliability and out-of-distribution robustness in large language models. It suggests that scaling or scratchpad supervision alone may not fix brittle arithmetic reasoning, affecting how practitioners design training and evaluation. The authors use black-box, model-agnostic metrics to analyze skill compositions and find that partially learned skills compete, producing characteristic mixing errors and weaker robustness under controlled distribution shifts. They further show that the same qualitative behavior persists in modern LLMs and is not mitigated by pure model scaling or scratchpad supervision.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Compositionality is the idea that complex skills are built from simpler ones in a hierarchical, rule-like way, as humans often learn arithmetic. Mechanistic interpretability is a subfield that reverse-engineers neural networks' internal computations to understand how they produce outputs. This paper combines these perspectives by training transformers on synthetic arithmetic and analyzing learning dynamics with model-agnostic metrics.

## [Constrained Bilevel RL via Approximate Lower-Level Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00282) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces a constrained bilevel reinforcement learning framework where the lower-level problem is a constrained Markov decision process with a generally parameterized policy. It randomizes reward and constraint values during lower-level training to obtain an unbiased gradient estimator for the upper-level objective without differentiating through lower-level updates. This work addresses a key challenge in bilevel reinforcement learning where standard hypergradient analyses fail due to non-Lipschitz and set-valued lower-level solutions. The proposed approach provides theoretical guarantees and sample complexity bounds, potentially impacting the RL theory community and applications requiring nested decision-making with constraints. The method establishes lower-level reward and feasibility guarantees, upper-level stationarity, and a total sample complexity of Õ(δ_ℓ^{-6} ε_o^{-2}), which becomes Õ(ε^{-8}) when δ_ℓ = ε_o = ε. The approach avoids differentiating through lower-level updates by randomizing rewards and constraints without changing their means.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Bilevel reinforcement learning involves two nested problems: an upper-level task that optimizes hyperparameters or rewards, and a lower-level task that solves a reinforcement learning problem. Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) extend standard MDPs by adding constraints on cumulative costs or risks, which is crucial for safety-critical applications. Hypergradient estimation is the technique of computing gradients through the lower-level optimization, but it becomes challenging when the lower-level solution is not unique or differentiable.

## [LEAP: Learning-Augmented Solver for Smooth Integer Programs with PAC Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02505) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces LEAP, a polynomial-time pipeline for smooth integer programs that uses a PAC-learnable oracle to predict Boolean assignments, then linearizes the objective around the prediction, solves an error-budgeted linear program, and rounds the solution. It establishes graceful degradation of approximation loss with prediction error and bounds the pseudo-dimension of the induced cost class to provide an end-to-end PAC-style generalization guarantee. This work bridges learning-augmented algorithms and integer programming by providing theoretical guarantees that separate the loss from imperfect predictions and the statistical error of learning, which could impact both optimization and machine learning communities. It offers a principled framework for using learned predictions in combinatorial optimization with performance guarantees. The guarantees apply to fixed-degree objectives, and the approximation loss is controlled by an error footprint that quantifies how mispredicted coordinates perturb local coefficients. Experiments on MAX-CUT and MAX-SAT show that LEAP substantially repairs imperfect predictions and scales to benchmarks with up to two million clauses.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Integer programming is a mathematical optimization framework where variables are restricted to integers, often used to model NP-hard combinatorial problems like MAX-CUT and MAX-SAT. PAC learning is a framework for analyzing machine learning algorithms, providing sample complexity guarantees for learning from data. Pseudo-dimension is a measure of the complexity of a class of real-valued functions, used to bound generalization error. Learning-augmented algorithms combine machine learning predictions with traditional algorithms to improve performance while maintaining worst-case guarantees.

The analysis reveals that residual connection layout fundamentally shapes convergence behavior, and ANCRe's adaptive reassignment yields consistently accelerated convergence, boosted performance, and enhanced depth efficiency across LLM, diffusion model, and deep ResNet pretraining. ## [New γ-weak θ-up-concavity framework unifies non-convex optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13506) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces γ-weak θ-up-concavity, a first-order condition for nonnegative monotone functions that strictly contains monotone DR-submodular and One-Sided Smooth (OSS) functions. It constructs a surrogate gradient and proves an upper-linearization inequality with a point-dependent approximation coefficient, enabling offline and online algorithms with improved guarantees. This framework unifies and generalizes two important classes of non-convex functions, potentially broadening the applicability of submodular optimization techniques in machine learning and combinatorial optimization. The improved approximation coefficients for OSS maximization over matroid constraints could lead to better algorithms for online learning and resource allocation problems. The approximation coefficient matches the optimal one for DR-submodular maximization and improves the best known coefficients for OSS maximization over matroid constraints when the OSS parameter is positive. The analysis relies on restricting actions to the closed convex hull of coordinate-wise maximal feasible points to ensure a uniformly positive coefficient.

One-Sided Smooth (OSS) functions generalize submodularity by allowing certain non-concavities, and have been studied for online maximization. This paper proposes a broader class that includes both, using a scaling function θ to model curvature that changes with solution size.

A new arXiv paper (2602.15919) proposes a retraining-free framework for assessing per-sample membership inference attack (MIA) vulnerability using only a single trained model and its last-layer representations. The authors derive a closed-form decomposition of individual MIA vulnerability into a population leverage score and a residual loss term in the linear setting, and extend it to deep networks via a surrogate score. This work enables efficient per-sample privacy risk assessment without the computational overhead of training shadow models, which is crucial for auditing and mitigating privacy leakage in machine learning deployments. It provides a theoretically grounded tool that outperforms loss and gradient-norm baselines, potentially impacting how organizations identify high-risk training points. The closed-form decomposition is mathematically guaranteed only in the linear case, and the extension to deep networks relies on a surrogate score operating on last-layer representations. Empirical evaluations across diverse datasets and architectures show the score outperforms baselines at identifying highest-risk points under state-of-the-art attacks.

## [Brief instruction boosts learning-oriented GenAI prompting in programming course](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16033) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A randomized controlled trial (N=431) in an introductory programming course found that all four instructional approaches—from a two-sentence reminder to a multi-step constructive task—produced learning-oriented GenAI prompting gains that persisted six weeks later, scaling from 8 to 51 percentage points with engagement level. Final exam performance did not differ between conditions. This provides the first rigorous RCT evidence that universities' GenAI-use policies can be translated into effective classroom practice with minimal instructional cost, giving instructors empirically calibrated options. It also suggests a boundary: improved prompting skill alone may not translate into better exam achievement, highlighting the need for further research on the pathway from prompting to learning outcomes. The study included a six-week end-of-semester follow-up and compared four conditions ranging from a two-sentence reminder (Condition 1) to a multi-step constructive task (Condition 4). Students in every condition self-reported sustained voluntary use of learning-oriented prompting, and confidence grew in step with skill, but the lack of exam differences places the possible boundary at the pathway from prompting skill to achievement.

A new arXiv paper (2603.00140v2) introduces Reachability-Aware Diffusion Steering (RADS), an offline-trained, sampling-time control framework that mitigates memorization in text-to-image diffusion models by learning a policy-conditioned reachability value function and using constrained reinforcement learning to perturb caption embeddings during denoising. Empirical results show RADS achieves a stronger Pareto frontier between generation diversity (SSCD), quality (FID), and alignment (CLIP) than state-of-the-art inference-time baselines. Memorization in text-to-image diffusion models is a known and important problem that can lead to copyright infringement and privacy leakage, and existing mitigation methods often sacrifice image quality or prompt alignment. RADS offers a principled sampling-time control approach that separates memorization mitigation from the pretrained model, potentially enabling safer deployment of diffusion models without retraining. RADS models the denoising process as a dynamical system and learns a reachability value function to estimate future memorization risk, then uses constrained RL to learn perturbations in the caption embedding space that steer trajectories away from memorized outputs. The controller is applied only at sampling time, so it does not modify the pretrained diffusion model, and the project page is available at https://s-karnik.github.io/rads-memorization-project-page/.

The paper introduces MAC, the first public conversion rate (CVR) prediction benchmark that provides labels generated by multiple attribution mechanisms, along with PyMAL, an open-source library of baseline methods for multi-attribution learning (MAL). It also presents Mixture of Asymmetric Experts (MoAE), a new MAL approach that substantially outperforms the existing state-of-the-art on MAC. Public CVR datasets have so far contained labels from only a single attribution mechanism, which has hindered research on MAL; MAC fills this data gap and, together with PyMAL, enables reproducible research and fair comparison of MAL methods. This is a valuable resource for the ad-tech and machine learning community, especially those working on conversion prediction and multi-task learning. The paper reports three key insights from experiments on MAC: MAL brings consistent gains especially for users with long conversion paths; performance growth scales with objective complexity in most settings, but adding auxiliary objectives is counterproductive when predicting first-click conversion targets; and two architectural principles are paramount—fully learning multi-attribution knowledge and fully leveraging it for the main task. MoAE is designed based on these principles and substantially surpasses the existing state-of-the-art MAL method.

## [LLMs Show Caste Bias in Matchmaking Evaluations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29288) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A controlled audit using real-world matrimonial profiles found that five LLM families (GPT, Gemini, Llama, Qwen, and BharatGPT) consistently rate same-caste matches up to about 30% higher than inter-caste matches on a 10-point scale, with ratings ordered by distance along the traditional caste hierarchy and an additional penalty for Dalit candidates. This is the first systematic evidence that LLMs reproduce caste-based stratification in a high-stakes social domain, suggesting that AI-mediated matchmaking could reinforce historical exclusion and that culturally grounded bias evaluation is urgently needed. The audit varied caste identity across Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra, and Dalit, and income across five buckets, prompting models to assess social acceptance, marital stability, and cultural compatibility from the perspective of a caste-identified bride or groom; the consistent hierarchical patterns across all five model families indicate that the bias is not limited to a single architecture or training corpus.

**Background**: The caste system is a hereditary social stratification historically divided into four varnas—Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (rulers/warriors), Vaishyas (traders), and Shudras (laborers)—with Dalits (formerly untouchables) outside and below this hierarchy. In South Asian matrimonial contexts, caste remains a central criterion for matchmaking, and LLMs are increasingly used to assess compatibility. A controlled audit is an experimental method that holds all variables constant except the one of interest (here, caste and income) to isolate causal effects of bias.

SLIDERS is a new LLM-based methodology that automatically assembles evidence tables for systematic reviews by using an autonomous coding agent that iteratively writes SQL to reconcile fragmented and inconsistent evidence across documents. SLIDERS extracts full-text excerpts as direct evidence or provenance for structured data, and its core reconciliation agent iteratively writes SQL to resolve inconsistencies and remove duplicates. The system outperforms all baselines on benchmarks within the LLM's context window, but scalability is tested on much larger corpora where accuracy drops to 55.2% on FinQ100, indicating challenges with very long documents.

## [AI Alignment as a Deterrence Game Between Solver and Auditor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01643) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.01643v4) models AI alignment as a strategic game between a solver and an auditor using law-and-economics deterrence theory, showing that stronger penalties can paradoxically reduce the auditor's incentive to inspect. It formalizes alignment as a fixed-point problem and proposes a bandit-based outer-loop method to search for reward profiles that induce both honest solver behavior and active auditor monitoring. This reframing highlights a subtle failure mode in agentic AI pipelines: oversight can erode precisely when it appears least needed, potentially allowing misbehavior to go undetected. The proposed reward-design method could inform safer post-training and verification practices for LLM-based systems, affecting researchers and practitioners building multi-agent or solver-auditor architectures. The model treats reward design as a bilevel optimization problem where rewards are judged by the behavioral equilibrium they induce, not their immediate semantic meaning. Experiments on an LLM coding pipeline show that adaptive reward profiles maintain oversight pressure and substantially reduce hallucinated incorrect attempts compared to static hand-designed rewards, though the work is a preprint without community discussion yet.

**Background**: Deterrence theory in law and economics models misconduct as a strategic response to the probability of detection and severity of punishment, and optimal enforcement often tolerates some underdeterrence to conserve resources. AI alignment research aims to steer AI systems toward intended goals, and fixed-point problems arise when the optimal action depends on the equilibrium behavior of other agents. Agentic AI pipelines often pair a solver that generates answers with an auditor or verifier that checks them, making the interaction between the two a natural target for mechanism design.

## [TIDE: Token-Level Credit Assignment via Entropy-Gated Bounded Deviation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03327) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TIDE introduces a critic-free reinforcement learning framework for LLMs that replaces sequence-level advantages with token-level importance using bounded Hellinger distance and entropy gating to improve credit assignment and exploration stability. On the Qwen2.5-32B backbone, TIDE achieves 60.0% and 46.0% Avg@32 accuracy on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025, respectively, outperforming strong baselines such as DAPO. This work addresses known limitations of GRPO, the leading critic-free RL algorithm for LLM alignment, by providing finer-grained token-level supervision and more stable exploration. If validated, it could influence future RLHF research and improve reasoning performance in large language models. TIDE replaces the unbounded KL penalty with the bounded Hellinger distance to avoid gradient explosion, and uses an entropy gating mechanism to scale deviation by predictive uncertainty, separating genuine reasoning breakthroughs from confident hallucinations. The method requires no value network and adds negligible overhead, with analyses supporting that entropy-gated deviation identifies pivotal reasoning steps.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a critic-free reinforcement learning algorithm introduced by DeepSeek for fine-tuning LLMs on reasoning tasks like math and code. It assigns a single sequence-level advantage to all tokens in a generated chain-of-thought and uses a KL penalty to constrain exploration, which can dilute token-level supervision and cause instability. Hellinger distance is a bounded metric between probability distributions, making it safer for regularization than unbounded KL divergence. Entropy gating uses the model's predictive uncertainty (entropy) to modulate updates, focusing learning on informative tokens.

GCAD replaces single-site residual-stream persona-vector injection with an attention-level intervention that extracts steering signals from system-prompt contributions to self-attention and applies token-level gating. The method is evaluated on persona-steering experiments, with code partially adapted from prior residual-stream steering projects and available on GitHub.

GAP's feature-level alignment uses a lightweight PCA-aligned latent head to map decoder outputs into input-compatible visual latents, while model-level alignment selectively applies latent supervision to examples where the base MLLM struggles. ## [Flexible Discrete Flow Matching Enables Variable-Length Biological Sequence Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10543) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces structured couplings, a latent edit-based rate parameterization, and latent classifier-free guidance for Discrete Flow Matching (DFM), enabling controllable variable-length biological sequence generation. It achieves state-of-the-art results on density estimation, unconditional and conditional DNA sequence generation, and peptide sequence generation. This work advances generative modeling for biological sequence design by addressing key limitations of DFM—uninformative couplings and fixed-length generation—potentially enabling more efficient exploration of protein and DNA sequence spaces under biological constraints. It could benefit researchers in AI-driven drug discovery and protein engineering. The structured coupling biases the source distribution toward biologically plausible regions without altering the flow objective or training procedure, while the latent edit-based parameterization models variable-length generation via edit operations conditioned on a shared global latent. A Dirichlet-prior temperature scaling provides test-time control over edit operations, and code is available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Discrete Flow Matching (DFM) is a generative modeling framework for discrete data that learns a transformation from a source distribution to a target distribution, generalizing continuous flow matching. Classifier-free guidance is a technique to trade off mode coverage and sample fidelity in conditional generative models without requiring a separate classifier. Biological sequence design involves navigating vast discrete spaces under evolutionary and biophysical constraints, where variable-length generation and fine-grained control are highly desirable.

## [Study quantifies subliminal behavioral transfer in language model distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11270) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2606.11270v3) systematically quantifies subliminal behavioral transfer ratios by steering two teacher models (Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) at varying strengths and distilling student models using only benign data. Evaluation on 100 JailbreakBench prompts with GPT-4.1 as judge reveals robust transfer with distinct scaling: Llama-2 shows a sharp threshold (τ = 0.25–0.32 beyond α = -0.15), while Qwen2.5 exhibits continuous and higher transfer (τ up to 0.61). This work provides the first systematic quantification of subliminal learning during distillation, showing that undesirable traits can leak from teacher to student even when training data is benign. These findings have direct implications for AI safety and alignment, as they suggest that data filtering alone may be insufficient to prevent the propagation of harmful behaviors in distilled models. The study uses activation steering to induce undesirable traits in teacher models, then distills with benign data and evaluates transfer on JailbreakBench prompts using GPT-4.1 as an automated judge. The transfer ratio τ varies by model: Llama-2 shows a threshold effect, while Qwen2.5 shows continuous scaling up to 0.61, indicating that transfer magnitude is model-specific and can be substantial.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data, meaning a student can acquire traits from a teacher even when the training data appears innocuous. Distillation, a common technique to compress large models into smaller ones, can thus propagate unintended traits, and data filtering may not prevent this. Activation steering is a method to control model behavior by adding vectors to internal activations, and JailbreakBench is a benchmark for evaluating jailbreak attacks and defenses.

## [NEXUS: Neural Energy Fields for Contact-Rich 3D Object Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15015) ⭐️ 7.0/10

NEXUS introduces a neural energy-field framework that models contact-rich 3D object dynamics by representing each object as a structural graph and constructing dynamic contact graphs, using Hamiltonian-inspired energy and Rayleigh-style dissipation terms to derive forces. It improves long-horizon accuracy over learned and physics-structured baselines and provides effective guidance for contact-rich video generation. This approach enables physically consistent motion composition of conservative and non-conservative effects in contact-rich scenes, which is valuable for physics-grounded video generation and simulation. It could improve the realism and controllability of generated 3D dynamics in AI-driven content creation and robotics. NEXUS composes conservative effects like gravity and elastic deformation as additive energy terms, models non-conservative effects such as damping and impact-induced energy loss with learned Rayleigh-style dissipation, and rolls out forces using a multi-substep semi-implicit integrator. It is evaluated on controlled trajectory benchmarks under varying mechanical properties and physical-effect compositions.

**Background**: Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) learn a scalar energy function from data and derive equations of motion via differentiation, ensuring energy conservation. The Rayleigh dissipation function is a classical mechanics tool that models velocity-proportional frictional forces by adding a dissipation term to the equations of motion. Contact-rich 3D object dynamics involve multiple objects interacting through contacts, deformation, and external forces, which is challenging for traditional learned dynamics models.

## [AI Sandboxes Get Threat Model and Measurement Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18532) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a threat model, taxonomy, and measurement framework for AI sandboxes, defining a sandbox apparatus, five overlapping archetypes, and fifteen claim-relative measurement dimensions. It introduces a weakest-link licensing rule that caps a deployment claim at its weakest necessary evidence dimension and applies the framework to four worked examples: driving, industrial control, tool-using agents, and vision-language-action manipulation. This framework helps researchers and practitioners determine what evidence bounded sandbox experiments can actually support and which assumptions require further validation before deployment, addressing a critical gap in AI safety evaluation. By connecting to standards and regulatory instruments, it could influence how AI sandbox results are interpreted in compliance and certification contexts. The framework covers both outward harm and corruption of the evaluation apparatus, and the weakest-link rule ensures that a deployment claim is only as strong as its weakest necessary evidence dimension. The four worked examples span diverse domains, demonstrating the framework's applicability to driving, industrial control, tool-using agents, and vision-language-action manipulation.

## [BELLS-O Benchmarks 33 LLM Supervision Systems on Operational Trade-offs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20668) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released BELLS-O, an independent operational benchmark that evaluates 33 LLM supervision systems from 17 developers — including specialized guardrails like Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma-2B, and Lakera Guard, plus frontier generalists such as GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Grok 4.1 Fast — jointly on detection rate, false-positive rate, latency, and cost across content moderation, jailbreak detection, and prompt-injection tasks. Existing benchmarks are often vendor-biased and omit cost and latency, so this vendor-neutral, operationally focused comparison gives practitioners concrete guidance for choosing safeguards under real deployment constraints and highlights that no single system wins across all use cases. A new arXiv paper (2607.07922v2) introduces 'adversarial decoys,' optimized image patches that redirect attention away from the true adversarial region, decoupling misclassification from defense evasion. This work reveals a fundamental limitation of using attention alone as an indicator of adversarial relevance, undermining a promising class of test-time defenses for ViTs. Adversarial patches are localized, visible perturbations that can cause misclassification, and recent test-time defenses try to detect them by suppressing tokens with abnormally high attention scores, based on the observation that adversarial tokens often attract substantial attention. This paper shows that this coupling can be broken by adding a separate decoy patch that manipulates the attention ranking.

Compared to Amazon's Isabelle Agent on miniF2F and NTP4VC-Pearl benchmarks, AoA reduces API cost by 2.3–4.7x, uses 2.9–6.9x fewer tokens, makes 3.9–8.9x fewer tool calls, and finishes 1.4–2.0x faster while solving more problems on the harder verification benchmark. This approach addresses a concrete pain point in LLM-based interactive theorem proving: high token consumption and fragility due to line-number-based state queries. By operating on ASTs, it enables the use of Minilang—a proof language that achieves state-of-the-art results but is too new for LLM training corpora—and could make formal verification more scalable and cost-effective. AoA drives the prover through a tree-edit model that fuses proof operations and states into a single proof tree, so each operation carries its own subgoal's state readable directly from the tree. The JSON-based AST representation is native to tool-calling LLMs, avoiding the need for separate line-number-based queries that shift with every edit.

**Background**: Interactive theorem proving (ITP) is essential for program verification and formalized mathematics, but manual effort limits scalability. Minilang is a minimalist proof language over Isabelle designed for neural theorem proving, but its novelty means LLMs have not been trained on it. AoA lifts the agent from source text to the abstract syntax tree (AST), using JSON representations that align with tool-calling LLMs.

Researchers introduce CamChoreo, the first benchmark for temporally grounded, compositional camera motion understanding, comprising 4,229 expert-annotated single-shot clips with 20 direction-aware labels, where nearly half of the segments contain compound camera motion. CamChoreo requires models to localize motion-consistent intervals and identify all active movements, with 20 direction-aware labels and compound motions in nearly half of segments. Supervised fine-tuning on the 43K corpus achieves 62.1/64.1 micro F1 with 4B/8B backbones, outperforming advanced closed-source VLMs, while CamDistill-8B also shows strong zero-shot transfer on CameraBench and CameraMotionVQA.

## [AgenticRAG-FP benchmark exposes failure attribution collapse in multi-hop RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20627) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces AgenticRAG-FP, an interventional benchmark that injects certified faults at specific hops in agentic RAG and re-executes the downstream trajectory to test whether post-hoc trace diagnosis can correctly attribute failures. In a dense Claude Haiku 4.5 sweep on three-hop MuSiQue questions, coverage-based diagnosis achieves 0.91 accuracy at hop 1 but 0.00 at hops 2 and 3, effectively degenerating into an earliest-hop heuristic that predicts hop 1 in 96% of failures. This work addresses a real and underexplored problem: in multi-hop agentic RAG, an early retrieval error may only surface as a wrong answer several hops later, making debugging difficult. The counterintuitive finding that a popular coverage-based diagnoser collapses to an earliest-hop rule has direct practical implications for how practitioners build and trust RAG debugging tools. In larger content-corruption runs, depth-2 exact-hop accuracy is 0.00 for coverage, 0.49 for an LLM judge, 0.59 for frozen-hop repair, and 0.14 for suffix regeneration (n=51), with the judge and frozen-hop repair not significantly different (exact McNemar p=0.33). At hops 2 and 3 in the structural sweep, the LLM judge and frozen-hop repair localize only 0.25 to 0.48 of failures, and the sample sizes are small (n=43, 36, 21 failed trajectories).

## [Private Dense Retrieval via Randomized Deep Hashing and Encrypted Reranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25735) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a private retrieval protocol that uses randomized learned deep hashing as a shortlist filter, combined with encrypted reranking and oblivious key transfer, to achieve private dense retrieval that closely matches full-corpus quality. With 200–500 candidates, it matches full-corpus retrieval across five zero-shot corpora ranging from 25K to 5.4M documents, and adds only 0.38 seconds (6.5%) to a 128-token Qwen3-32B RAG pipeline on the 2.68M-passage NQ corpus over a 10-Gbps link. This work makes privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented generation and semantic search practical at scale by avoiding the cost of full-corpus cryptographic search while preserving retrieval quality. It could benefit hosted RAG providers and users who need to hide queries and results while enforcing document-level authorization. The released code satisfies directional metric differential privacy (DP) and substantially reduces embedding-inversion and property-inference leakage. The approach repurposes learned deep hashing as a private filter: a randomized binary code points the provider to a short candidate list, while encrypted reranking and oblivious key transfer protect the precise query and final selection.

## [Coalitional Alignment Enables Safe Delegation to Misaligned AI Reviewers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15803) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces k-robust coalitional alignment, a condition on a panel of reviewing agents that is weaker than individual alignment yet necessary and sufficient to guarantee that a principal fares at least as well as under a baseline policy when delegating authorization decisions. It shows that a threshold rule tolerating k disapprovals is safe exactly when, after removing any k reviewers, the principal's utility is a nonnegative combination of the remaining reviewers' utilities plus a term nonnegative on every feasible proposal, and extends this characterization to sequential control in discounted MDPs. This work addresses the attention bottleneck in human oversight of long-running AI agents by showing that review can be safely delegated to potentially misaligned AI reviewers, which could make scalable oversight practical without requiring every reviewer to be individually aligned. It provides a precise theoretical criterion for when collective review is sound, relevant to AI safety and multi-agent control. The characterization lifts to sequential control: in a discounted MDP with an arbitrary proposer agent, safety at every state is both necessary and sufficient for the induced policy to match or improve on the baseline. When reviewers vote strategically, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees every Nash equilibrium is safe under unanimous approval, whereas more permissive thresholds can admit unsafe equilibria even with individually aligned reviewers; experiments with existing reviewer models show collective review can remain sound without an aligned individual.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: AI alignment refers to steering AI systems toward intended goals, preferences, or ethical principles; an agent is aligned if it advances the principal's objectives. Long-running AI agents create a control problem because each action changes state and affects future actions, so if an agent is not fully aligned, consequential actions need approval before execution. Delegating review to other AI agents seems circular because reviewers may themselves be misaligned, and human approval at every step makes human attention a bottleneck.

## [Weight-Perturbing Importance Sampling Estimates Rare Agent Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24969) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.24969v2) proposes 'iterative unalignment,' an importance sampling method that perturbs a language model's weights to build a differentiable proposal distribution for estimating rare catastrophic event probabilities in stochastic agents. Evaluated on ~120M and ~2.6B parameter models across 300+ rare events as rare as 10^-9, the estimator achieved over 800x compute-weighted efficiency gains over naive Monte Carlo for events below 10^-7 probability. As autonomous agents are deployed more widely, even extremely rare output events can be catastrophic, so safe deployment depends on knowing how often they occur rather than merely whether they can. This work offers a practical, gradient-based way to quantify such tail risks, which is directly relevant to AI safety evaluation and reliability engineering for LLM-based agents. The proposal is itself a differentiably parameterized language model, enabling gradient-based search over weight space, with an objective combining a differentiable surrogate for event amplification and an adaptive regularization scheme that balances amplification against estimator stability. All reference probabilities were independently estimated, and code is released at github.com/namkoong-lab/iterative-unalignment.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Estimating the probability of rare events by naive Monte Carlo simulation is computationally prohibitive because the events occur so infrequently that enormous numbers of samples are needed. Importance sampling addresses this by drawing samples from a proposal distribution that makes rare events more likely, then reweighting the results; classical methods such as the cross-entropy method iteratively tune such proposals. In language-model agents, rare events arise from coordinated changes across a context-dependent chain of conditional distributions, making effective proposals hard to construct.

## [Paper Argues Audits Should Target Agent Scaffolds, Not Just Model Checkpoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34924) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv position paper (2609.34924v2) argues that self-improvement audits for AI coding agents should track changes to the scaffold—tools, tests, and task breakdown—rather than only whether the model's weights were retrained or frozen. The authors propose, but do not run, an experiment to test whether the scaffold can grow even with frozen weights, and they present descriptive evidence from a public coding benchmark and 401 development sessions showing diminishing returns from repeated revision. This paper challenges the common assumption that a frozen model guarantees stable behavior, arguing that scaffold rewrites can raise the ceiling of improvement and therefore must be audited. If adopted, it could reshape evaluation and safety practices for agentic coding systems, affecting AI safety researchers, agent developers, and benchmark designers. The paper distinguishes three often-conflated mechanisms: more search within a fixed setup, retraining the model during use (which can raise the ceiling), and rewriting the scaffold, which sits between them. It also notes that adding more agents does not lift the ceiling—picking the best of several agents' answers reaches the best single agent's ceiling exactly, and majority voting only helps if agents fail on different tasks; in their tests, 30 agents from one model family failed together, with a majority failing 23/55 (42%) of tasks.

## [PhaseBreak: Proactive Temporal Protection Against Unauthorized Image-to-Video Animation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33070) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PhaseBreak introduces a white-box spectral retiming perturbation that protects images from unauthorized image-to-video (I2V) diffusion animation by rearranging the temporal order of intermediate denoiser features rather than merely attenuating them. Evaluated on Stable Video Diffusion and DynamiCrafter, protected images produce greater short-term motion variation and lower temporal regularity, impeding stable motion customization. This work offers a new proactive defense concept for individuals who share images online and want to prevent them from being animated without consent, addressing a growing privacy and content-ownership concern as I2V models become more accessible. It also advances the broader field of adversarial protection for generative models by showing that temporal ordering, not just feature strength, can be exploited for disruption. PhaseBreak operates along the true temporal axis and uses a subject-aware mask to confine the protective perturbation to the depicted subject, preserving the sharing workflow while disrupting downstream motion generation. The method is white-box, meaning it assumes access to the target diffusion model's internals, which may limit its practical applicability against unknown or black-box I2V systems.

**Background**: Image-to-video diffusion models can animate a single portrait or photograph, enabling shared images to be repurposed for motion synthesis without the subject's authorization. Proactive visual protection aims to prevent this by applying a bounded, imperceptible perturbation to an image before it is released, so that the sharing workflow is preserved but downstream motion generation is disrupted. Existing spectral disruption objectives globally attenuate temporal representations, providing limited control over subtle or spatially localized motion. PhaseBreak builds on the insight that generated dynamics depend not only on temporal feature strength but also on the order in which feature events occur.

## [PACK3D decouples memory layout from attention geometry in packed 3D transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38694) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PACK3D introduces a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry in packed 3D token sequences, using axial RoPE at token-grid coordinates and pooled summaries to achieve repacking equivariance. On Allen WTC-11 microscopy at 262k tokens, repacking validation volumes costs a packed-sequence RoPE control 0.048 macro Dice on average, while PACK3D changes by only 0.0001. This work reveals that sequence-indexed positional mechanisms can learn rasterization artifacts rather than object geometry, a subtle failure mode invisible on the training layout. It matters for practitioners building 3D transformers for vision and scientific imaging, since it offers a way to make models robust to arbitrary token packing choices without sacrificing accuracy. PACK3D attends exactly within a coordinate-defined neighborhood, sees the whole field through pooled summaries, and rotates queries and keys with axial RoPE at token-grid coordinates; because keys are rotated before pooling, each query-to-summary logit is a weighted sum of query-key terms at the summarized tokens' displacements. A full PACK3D layer runs within 7-31% of window-attention latency while adding a global pathway, and it exceeds a parameter-matched 3D U-Net by 0.009 Dice over six seeds.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Packing a 3D field into a token sequence gives each token two indices: a spatial coordinate and a position in memory, and layouts such as raster, Morton (Z-order), and block-contiguous change only the latter. Standard positional encodings indexed by sequence position can therefore learn the storage order rather than the underlying geometry. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes position by rotating query and key vectors before the attention dot product, and its axial variant applies independent rotations along each spatial axis to capture multi-axis structure. Equivariance means that transforming the input (here, repacking the tokens) produces a predictably transformed output, which is a desirable property for robust 3D models.

A new arXiv paper (2611.06486v2) demonstrates that model merging does not require all experts to be trained at the same LoRA rank. By training 36 experts across three domains at four ranks and three model scales, the authors show that using each domain's own best rank can improve multi-domain accuracy by up to 1.8 percentage points for averaging and utility-based selection methods. This finding challenges the standard practice of uniform LoRA ranks in model merging, potentially allowing practitioners to optimize each expert's rank independently and achieve better multi-domain performance without retraining. Choosing components by their effect on loss instead keeps all experts and leaves accuracy nearly flat across an 8x rank range (0.7 pp vs. 6.7 pp for TIES at 4B scale).

## [Retina: Open-Source Framework for Real-Time Transactional Lakehouse Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12169) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Retina is a new open-source data synchronization framework that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses, achieving 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million rows/s linear-scalable throughput. This addresses a key challenge for real-time analytics in lakehouses, where existing systems trade off data freshness, query performance, and resource efficiency; Retina's approach could significantly improve real-time data ingestion and analytics for lakehouse users. Retina is implemented and open-sourced, and evaluations show it outperforms state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead.

**Background**: Lakehouses combine the scalability of data lakes with the ACID transactions and schema enforcement of data warehouses, but their read-optimized immutable file storage makes real-time data changes challenging. The RUM conjecture states that data systems must trade off among read overhead, update overhead, and memory overhead, which complicates achieving all three simultaneously.

## [HumanSightBench: New Benchmark Exposes MLLM Visual Perception Gaps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12305) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces HumanSightBench, a benchmark of 2,876 short-answer visual questions across 7 perceptual categories and 21 subcategories, designed to be easy for humans but hard for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The best pass@3 score among eight evaluated MLLMs is only 65.6%, and no model exceeds 27.5% on the Counting category. This benchmark isolates visual perception from other skills like reasoning and knowledge, revealing capability gaps that overall scores hide. It provides a targeted evaluation tool that could guide future training and held-out evaluation for vision-language models. Items are included only if they pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering, which reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The benchmark defines errors as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) combine language models with visual encoders to process both text and images, and they excel on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmarks. However, their performance on simple perceptual tasks that humans easily solve remains unclear because end-to-end evaluations mix multiple skills. HumanSightBench aims to isolate visual perception by constructing questions that are human-easy by design and model-hard by evaluation.

## [Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13223) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents the first blind, multi-seed measurement of full reasoning-history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, testing nine open-weight reasoning models across three rendering conditions, three seeds, and 794 tasks. The same deletion causes performance changes ranging from -3.9 to +51.3 points depending on the model, and for one model re-dosed from 0 to 100 percent deletion, the reading varies by at most 1.5 points. This finding establishes deletion sensitivity as a measurable model-level property, meaning routing and aggregation systems should treat it as prior information rather than an invisible default cost. Practitioners building multi-turn agent systems across multiple model providers need to account for how stripping reasoning history affects task performance differently per model. The study used 94k ShareGPT conversations, finding that 73 percent of user interactions span multiple turns, and employed the official checker for evaluation. A two-cell screen—one retention run and one deletion run—can re-read a retrained or re-released model at the cost of two runs, making the measurement practical for deployment decisions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Reasoning models generate a reasoning trace at each turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read this history. Upstream providers bind each trace to its issuer, so when a request is forwarded across issuers, the history is deleted—a common scenario in multi-provider agent systems. ShareGPT is a dataset of real user-assistant conversations often used to study multi-turn interaction patterns.

## [CAMG-II and CAMP-II: On-Policy Distillation for File-Based Memory in Long-Horizon Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14009) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces CAMG-II, a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual, each providing Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace so policies can use files as memory across context replacements. It also presents CAMP-II, which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous on-policy distillation (OPD) from a frozen teacher, achieving 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline and generalizing to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2. This work addresses a key bottleneck in long-horizon LLM agents: deciding what to write down and read back when interaction histories exceed the active context. By showing that OPD weakens when memory interfaces fall outside pre-training and that file-based memory learned via OPD transfers to external benchmarks, it offers a practical path toward more capable coding agents. The paper identifies a two-sided weakness in OPD for memory control: the teacher cannot guide an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. CAMP-II mitigates this by using a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations and fully asynchronous training across five environments.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Long-horizon tasks are tasks whose success depends on a sequence of interdependent decisions, and their interaction histories often exceed an LLM's active context window. On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training method where a student model learns from a teacher's feedback on its own sampled actions, combining the reliability of on-policy training with dense reward signals. Memory control—deciding when and what to persist or retrieve—is increasingly framed as part of the agent's policy, but prior work relies on memory tools and compaction protocols that may not appear in either model's pre-training.

## [PASE: Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14019) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PASE (Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution) is a new framework that evolves LLM agent skills by associating them with executable programs, separating reusable procedural logic from natural-language descriptions so that updates can target executable components directly. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show PASE consistently outperforms all baselines by over 2.8%, with greater evolutionary stability and generalization. Existing skill-evolution methods represent skills as monolithic natural-language documents, which intertwine procedural logic with descriptive knowledge and make skills hard to maintain and evolve. By making procedural logic editable and patchable as code, PASE addresses a real maintainability bottleneck and could make agent skill libraries more robust and easier to update over time. PASE iteratively evolves skills by distilling trajectory-derived experience into editable programs rather than repeatedly rewriting natural-language skill documents, enabling targeted patches to executable components. The reported gains exceed 2.8% over baselines across diverse models and benchmarks, and the authors state that all data and code will be released via GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: LLM agents often use skills—reusable knowledge artifacts, typically written as natural-language documents—to solve complex interactive tasks without changing model parameters. Recent work distills experience from agent execution trajectories and evolves skills based on downstream task feedback, but representing skills purely in natural language mixes procedural steps with descriptive knowledge, making maintenance difficult. PASE draws on program synthesis ideas to encode reusable procedural logic as executable programs that can be patched independently.

## [Systematic review finds fragmented evaluation of ambient AI scribes in healthcare](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14284) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A systematic review of 54 recent evaluation studies of ambient AI scribes in healthcare identifies ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics, operationalized in 96 different ways, with 35 (36%) used by only a single study. Documentation efficiency and time dominate assessment, appearing in 44 of 54 studies, while safety and clinical outcomes are least consistently assessed. The lack of standardized metrics makes it difficult to compare findings or cumulatively synthesize evidence across studies, hindering rigorous evaluation of tools that are rapidly moving from pilots to enterprise-wide deployment. This review highlights the need for a holistic, standardized, multi-dimensional set of metrics to assess ambient scribes' impact on documentation burden, clinician experience, and patient outcomes. The metrics used rely heavily on self-report and are inconsistently operationalized, limiting comparability; ripple effects on the broader care system, such as impact on patients' care outcomes, redistribution of work, changes in billing and coding intensity, and downstream use of notes by other clinicians, are rarely assessed.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Ambient AI scribes are voice-enabled AI tools that record, transcribe, and summarize patient-physician conversations to generate clinical notes, promising to reduce documentation burden and improve clinician experience. They have moved rapidly from experimental pilots to enterprise-wide deployment across health systems, but there are no agreed-upon protocols or standardized metrics for assessing their performance. Systematic reviews aim to synthesize evidence across studies, but fragmented measurement practices can undermine their ability to draw cumulative conclusions.

## [Zugwise: Chess Engine Techniques Digitize Handwritten Scoresheets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14544) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Zugwise reframes handwritten chess scoresheet digitization as a game reconstruction problem, using computer-chess machinery like quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, and pin detection to detect plausible-but-wrong moves. In oracle replay of two tournament sections, adding the second player's sheet as evidence reduced silent errors from 16 to 1 and from 50 to 13. This approach addresses silent errors that legality-only pipelines miss, which can corrupt all subsequent moves in a game. It could improve the accuracy of digitizing historical chess records and offers a three-way adjudication protocol for domains where no single record is ground truth. The system uses a Needleman-Wunsch merge to align the two players' sheets, and a backward search traces late symptoms to their cause. Two learned signals, CTC re-scoring and a Maia-style human-move prior, raise the correct fix's top-rank rate from 58.8% to 78.0%, and the system runs entirely in the browser, free and offline-capable.

However, a misread that results in a legal but wrong move is silent and can propagate errors. Computer-chess techniques like quiescence search (evaluating tactical sequences), static exchange evaluation (assessing material outcomes of exchanges), and pin detection (identifying constrained pieces) are used here to assess whether a move is plausible for a human to have written.

## [Food Critic: Auditable Agentic Visualization for Restaurant Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15843) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers present Food Critic, an agentic visualization system that combines public health inspection records with crowd review data to support diners' restaurant decisions. The system compares three grounding conditions—a database-only ReAct agent, a retrieval-augmented agent with food-safety regulations, and an ontology-guided agent producing structured hypotheses and typed evidence—and externalizes the agent's reasoning as inspectable visual evidence. As LLM agents are increasingly embedded in visualization and decision-support tools, this work addresses the critical question of whether users can inspect how an answer is grounded rather than merely whether it is useful. Its approach to visual provenance and auditable reasoning could inform the design of trustworthy GenAI decision-support interfaces beyond restaurant safety. The evaluation tests multiple LLM models across several use cases under each of the three grounding configurations, with the ontology-guided variant producing typed evidence intended to make reasoning more structured and inspectable. As an arXiv preprint, the work is a research prototype and its practical deployment or user-study validation is not described in the abstract.

## [Society-Centered AI Governance Framework Evaluated in North Carolina](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16173) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces the Society-Centered AI Governance Framework, which assesses AI policy instruments by whether individuals can receive notice, challenge decisions, and see corrections. It was evaluated in North Carolina through interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members before and after the state's 2026 AI roadmap, plus a provision-level analysis of 49 AI governance documents from 19 states. The framework offers a shared language to assess AI policy while it is still being formed, focusing on recourse before harm occurs. It could help policymakers, researchers, and the public evaluate whether AI governance provides actionable rights, not just principles. The evaluation found visibility-first governance in North Carolina: visibility duties are in effect, notice exists as an agency duty without an invokable right, and AI-specific challenge and correction remain advisory. The authors identify 'legitimacy before protection' as a testable risk and note that federal preemption proposals focus on AI development, leaving recourse for state systems likely a state decision.

**Background**: AI governance research has documented outputs like principles, strategies, registers, and audits, but lacks shared language to understand policy during its formation. The title references Niti and Nyaya from Indian political thought, where Niti denotes ideal institutional rules and Nyaya denotes lived justice outcomes, a distinction used by Amartya Sen. North Carolina established an AI Leadership Council in November 2025 to advance AI literacy, governance, and deployment.

Researchers trained Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agents on increasingly large sets of procedurally generated Super Mario Bros. levels and evaluated them on 1000 held-out test levels, finding that more training levels generally improved generalization. This work provides empirical evidence that scaling up procedurally generated training levels can improve generalization to unseen levels for model-free agents, addressing a key open question in game AI. The study uses 1000 held-out test levels for evaluation and finds that increasing the number of distinct PCG-generated training levels generally improves unseen-level performance. DRAIL fine-tuning increases action-level human-likeness while preserving much of the persona induced by PPO pretraining, though the preservation is partial and the approach is incremental rather than a paradigm shift.
