## [SAGE-QA: Semantic-Aware Evaluation for Closed-Context QA on SQuAD 2.0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16300) ⭐️ 6.0/10

SAGE-QA introduces a multi-tiered evaluation framework that combines reference-based Semantic Equivalence Scoring (SES) and passage-based Re-Validation Scoring (RVS) to better assess generative LLMs on SQuAD 2.0, moving beyond Exact Match (EM). On 10,000 validation examples, zero-shot Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro achieve 85.21 and 86.66 EM, while fine-tuned open-weight models reach up to 94.24 EM, with fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B surpassing the previous best known EM. Exact Match is overly strict for generative LLMs, as it penalizes valid paraphrases and alternative passage-supported answers, so SAGE-QA provides a more nuanced evaluation that separates lexical divergence from factual errors. This could influence how QA systems are benchmarked and lead to fairer comparisons between models, especially as generative models become more prevalent. SAGE-QA computes EM and decision-matrix F1 from TP, TN, FP, and FN counts, and uses an external LLM judge for SES and RVS; on frontier models, SES scores are 92.81 for Claude Opus 4.6 and 91.67 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, while hybrid RVS scores are 97.96 and 98.02. The framework is evaluated on a fixed set of 10,000 SQuAD 2.0 validation examples, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning adds 21.19 to 34.06 EM points for open-weight models.

## [Prompt Optimization Narrows Capacity Gaps in Small Language Model Routers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16414) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.16414) investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity in small language models (SLMs) when deciding which inference capabilities to activate. Using Qwen2.5 routers from 1.5B to 14B parameters and five prompting strategies, the study finds that prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, but RAG and web search still benefit more from larger models. This work shows that smaller routers with optimized prompts can achieve downstream quality comparable to enabling all capabilities while drastically reducing token consumption (68.7%) and latency (80.5%), which could make multi-capability LLM systems more efficient and cost-effective. It also highlights that classification F1 alone is insufficient for router selection, as error profiles and routing overhead matter. The 14B router achieved a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408 versus 0.8418 when all capabilities were enabled, while cutting average downstream token consumption from 8,837 to 2,764 and median latency from 9.79 to 1.91 seconds. However, these savings exclude router overhead, which increases with router capacity and was measured separately.

The paper introduces First-Person Semantic Response Grids (FPSRG), a method that builds retrievable LLM configurations to simulate heterogeneous users by combining shared post-training, dimension-specific control vectors, and a searchable catalog of measured profile scores. Experiments on Qwen models show that refinement increases the mean five-axis composite control span from 30.75 to 40.45, and a five-level vector catalog covers 92.2% of fixed targets within a 25-75 target region. The method uses per-token configuration routing, continuous batching, and isolated caches to support parallel measurement of different profiles. Coverage improves with denser measurement: three-, five-, and nine-level catalogs achieve 71.2%, 92.2%, and 94.6% coverage respectively, and combining the vector catalog with a prompt catalog increases coverage to 98.7%.

## [Quantization disagreement as an error signal for small language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16478) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.16478) tests whether disagreement between an 8-bit copy and a lower-precision copy of the same small model can serve as a per-question error score for abstention, escalation, or re-asking. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B across 8,398 multiple-choice questions, the best disagreement score reached AUROC 0.684 on the 0.6B model, only +0.001 over the entropy baseline, and showed no gain on the 1.7B model. If reliable, quantization disagreement would offer a cheap, training-free uncertainty signal for local models, requiring only one extra forward pass over fewer bytes. The modest results suggest this signal is not quantization-specific and is often beaten by simpler alternatives like option-order shuffling or routing to a larger model, tempering expectations for deployment. The study simulates round-to-nearest quantization with per-group scales (3–6 bits, groups of 32–256) and finds that Gaussian weight noise at matched error energy is about as informative as rounding, so the signal is not specific to quantization. An extra 8-bit pass that shifts option order outperforms disagreement by +0.049 AUROC over entropy at about a third more weight traffic, and routing to a larger model on free entropy beats both extra-pass scores at equal total traffic.

**Background**: Quantization reduces the numerical precision of a model's weights, shrinking memory and speeding inference, but it can change individual answers. Applied to QuaRot, it achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 5.88 and an average zero-shot reasoning accuracy of 72.73, surpassing SpinQuant on LLaMA3-70B. This work addresses a key bottleneck in low-bit LLM quantization—massive outlier activations that degrade performance—by providing a lightweight, drop-in improvement compatible with any Hadamard-based quantization method. It enables more efficient inference without additional matrix multiplication, potentially broadening the adoption of quantized LLMs. SignRot requires only a single calibration forward pass and adds only element-wise sign flips at inference, avoiding the need for a full matrix multiplication. It is paired with asymmetric activation quantization to absorb the mean shift caused by aligned outliers.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Quantization compresses large language models (LLMs) to reduce memory and accelerate inference, but outlier activations—especially massive ones—can severely degrade low-bit representation. Rotation-based methods like QuaRot and SpinQuant use randomized Hadamard transforms to spread outliers, but when a single massive outlier dominates, the distribution can fragment into empty bins, hurting uniform quantization. SpinQuant learns rotations via training but cannot be applied at the down-projection input where rotation must be online due to preceding nonlinearity, because a learned dense matrix would require a full matrix multiplication instead of the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform.

## [Frozen ASL Pose Encoder Boosts Low-Resource Sign Language Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16621) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A study evaluated a frozen pose encoder trained on American Sign Language (ASL-Citizen) on six low-resource sign language datasets (Turkish, Russian, Indian, Argentinian, Pakistani, Sri Lankan) for sign retrieval with one or four enrolled clips per sign. With one enrolled clip, the encoder retrieved the correct sign first in 36.4–80.7% of queries, outperforming the best learning-free method (angle-based DTW, 16.0–69.6%) and an ASL-trained OpenHands graph network (six-target mean 39.3%). It could enable cross-lingual sign language retrieval tools for low-resource communities and inform future encoder design choices. Ablation experiments show that a per-pair InfoNCE objective outperforms supervised contrastive and cross-entropy training, and blocking attention between body, left hand, and right hand inside the encoder raises accuracy by up to 5.1 points; the best configuration reaches 68.0% one-shot accuracy (vs. 59.0% for the reference encoder). On the CISLR Indian Sign Language dictionary (4,765 words, one video per word), the encoders achieve 17.3–19.0% top-1 accuracy, above the 16.8% RGB baseline, and embedding geometry (spherical, Euclidean, hyperbolic) has only a minor effect (≤1.6 points difference) except for a hyperbolic token-attention head trained with InfoNCE, which is 1.4–2.0 points worse.

## [CAFIN: CUDA Kernel Fusion Speeds Up AdaFisher Second-Order Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14589) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CAFIN is a GPU-native CUDA kernel fusion framework that accelerates AdaFisher's Fisher Information Matrix-based second-order optimization by fusing preconditioner construction, EMA updates, and parameter updates into shared-memory and register-resident kernels. Experiments on ResNet-18 across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet show up to 78.4% lower isolated FIM construction latency and 2.1–26.9% lower optimizer-step latency, while eliminating about 18.91 MB of intermediate GPU memory allocations per step. Second-order optimizers like AdaFisher can improve training efficiency but are often bottlenecked by GPU execution overhead from sequential kernel launches and memory traffic. CAFIN demonstrates that kernel fusion can substantially reduce this overhead without changing the optimizer's mathematical formulation, making second-order methods more practical for deep learning training on consumer-grade GPUs. The framework fuses FIM preconditioner construction, EMA updates, gradient preconditioning, momentum accumulation, weight decay, and parameter updates into unified CUDA kernels, using shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation, and in-place operations. Numerical validation confirms consistency within FP32 tolerance, and convergence accuracy remains comparable across datasets and random seeds, though speedups vary by GPU (GTX 1660 Ti and RTX 3060 Laptop).

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Second-order optimizers use curvature information, often derived from the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), to precondition gradients and speed up training compared to first-order methods like SGD or Adam. AdaFisher is a recent adaptive second-order optimizer that approximates the FIM using a diagonal block-Kronecker structure and exponential moving averages to reduce cost. However, its PyTorch implementation launches many sequential CUDA kernels, causing overhead from kernel launches, intermediate tensor allocations, and repeated memory accesses. CUDA kernel fusion merges multiple kernels into one to reduce these overheads and improve on-chip data reuse.

## [Study pinpoints which code fixes which foundation-model errors in bitemporal inventory simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14671) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.14671) presents a controlled component diagnostic on an exactly solvable lost-sales inventory environment, running 36,672 independently rescored requests across twelve configurations of closed and open-weight models. It finds that canonical input removes report-selection error, exact continuation removes rollout error, neither repairs the other, and asking models to reason harder is no substitute and can even collapse performance under a forced-answer-call interface. This work offers practitioners a systematic map of which exact-code remedies address which error types for which models, showing that weak and strong models fail in separable ways. It also provides evidence that for some model-provider pairs the tool-calling interface confounds reasoning evaluation, which matters for anyone benchmarking or deploying foundation models in operational reporting pipelines. The study uses a forced-answer-call interface as a control with protocols frozen before calls, and reports that under a forced answer call high effort collapses GPT-5.4 mini and DeepSeek V4 Pro, on its provider the forced call disables reasoning for DeepSeek V4 Flash, and at high effort gpt-oss exhausts its output budget. Every request is released alongside the paper to support reproducibility.

**Background**: Bitemporal data modeling tracks two timelines for each record: when an event actually happened and when its report arrived, allowing later reports to revise earlier ones. MITRA-Swarm is a multi-agent architecture that injects explicit linguistic structure into foundation models for classical Sanskrit machine translation, achieving an MQM score of 85.90 versus a monolithic baseline of 85.27 on a 1,000-verse benchmark. The system uses specialized agents for Sandhi splitting, compound handling, and ellipsis restoration, along with dual judges for routing and reporting. This work demonstrates that explicit linguistic structure can yield measurable improvements in low-resource, morphologically rich languages like Sanskrit, potentially informing translation systems for other classical or low-resource languages. The dual-judge design also addresses self-evaluation bias in LLM-based assessment. The full swarm improves MQM by +0.63 (p_adj=0.0018) over the baseline, with discourse restoration alone contributing +0.44 MQM, but at roughly 9x the per-verse inference cost. ## [Entropy-Based View Selection in Test-Time Adaptation Fails to Identify Correct Views](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14686) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new audit of test-time adaptation for vision-language models shows that view selection, not gradient updates, accounts for almost all accuracy gains, and that entropy-based scoring ranks correct views no better than chance when predictions are wrong. The authors propose using the fraction of the original image retained by each crop as a simple, unused signal that improves accuracy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets over entropy. This work challenges the dominant reliance on entropy for view selection in test-time adaptation pipelines, suggesting that a simple, overlooked signal from the augmentation process can be more effective. It could lead to more robust and efficient adaptation methods for vision-language models like CLIP, impacting practitioners deploying these models under distribution shift. The study holds other pipeline stages fixed and finds that entropy recovers only about one-twentieth of the accuracy recovered by an oracle over the same views, across two image encoders and with a control ruling out statistical artifacts. The proposed crop-retention fraction improves accuracy on 14 of 15 datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest scoring function tested, and a pre-method measurement predicts which datasets benefit.

Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to adapt pre-trained models during inference without labeled data or backpropagation. A common TTA approach generates randomly cropped and flipped copies (views) of each test image and combines their predictions, using prediction entropy to select the most confident views. Researchers propose RACE, a risk-aware control framework that maps predicted action-failure probability and task criticality to adaptive SINR targets for uplink transmission in 6G physical AI edge inference. A slow-timescale LLM proposes task requirements for deterministic validation, while a fast hybrid actor selects inference configurations and transmit power, achieving an 11% improvement in the average accuracy-latency-energy objective over fixed-high-SINR control with near-zero constraint outage. RACE combines deadline-derived SINR requirements with risk-aware adaptive targets, uses an LLM for slow-timescale task requirement proposals validated deterministically, and employs a fast hybrid actor for resource control complemented by analytical receive beamforming and finite power restoration. Simulations show 11% improvement in the average accuracy-latency-energy objective with near-zero constraint outage.

Mach2 is a new platform that couples Eigen orchestration with deterministic, lint-like checks on tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts in LLM agent workflows. It represents domain requirements as executable predicates, where mandatory failures block advancement and diagnostic findings are retained for correction or review. This work addresses a key limitation of LLM agents—that prompting alone cannot guarantee compliance with natural-language operating rules—by providing a rule-gated execution model with measurable criteria for rule compliance, engineering validity, and cross-endpoint task continuity. Mach2 incorporates user-specified test-driven development (TDD), CodeGrapher's abstract-syntax-tree analysis, and history-guided evolutionary search as complementary verification and optimization mechanisms. It also generates task-specific agent packages for execution through independently selected endpoints, with the originating harness validating returned artifacts against declared interfaces and evidence requirements without assuming continuous supervision; model-internal-knowledge (MIK) dependencies are recorded separately from source-grounded and test-supported findings.

## [Hint-Informed Self-Distillation Boosts Reasoning Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14931) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Hint-Informed Self-Distillation (HISD), a method that uses offline-generated segment hints to perform token-level credit assignment in reasoning segmentation. Under a unified training protocol, HISD improves ReasonSeg test gIoU and cIoU over a reproduced DPAD baseline by 3.00 and 3.55 percentage points, respectively, while reducing the average token count of valid reasoning spans by 80.17 to 91.83 percent. This work addresses a key limitation in reinforcement learning for reasoning segmentation: trajectory-level rewards cannot indicate which tokens provide relevant visual evidence. By enabling token-level credit assignment, HISD encourages concise yet disambiguating reasoning, potentially improving both accuracy and efficiency in vision-language models for segmentation tasks. HISD uses an external model to generate Segment Hints offline, which organize target identity, discriminative attributes, confusable objects, and anchoring paths. A hint-conditioned exponential moving average teacher scores the student's trajectories, and the teacher-to-student evidence ratio adjusts only the magnitudes of positive group-relative advantages, leaving nonpositive advantages unchanged; the student requires neither hints nor a teacher at inference.

## [CoLaX: Context-Aware Local Explanations for Time Series Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15067) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CoLaX introduces a context-aware post-hoc explanation framework for time series classifiers that conditions local shapelet relevance on a learned representation of the full sequence, using global context to produce sample-specific prototype weights and a temporally resolved signal that reweights the local activation map. On synthetic benchmarks where identical motifs change relevance across contexts, CoLaX improves AUPRC over the strongest baseline by 30% on average, and achieves the highest AUPRC on real-world ECG data. This work addresses a key limitation of existing time series explanation methods, which score local patterns in isolation and ignore global temporal context, and could improve trust and interpretability for applications like clinical ECG monitoring where the same motif can mean different things under different regimes. The strong empirical gains suggest that context-aware attribution is a promising direction for explainable AI in time series. The method builds on shapelet-driven Shapley attribution, where context-conditioned segments serve as players in a Shapley game whose values come only from the frozen black-box classifier. Ablations indicate that the gains stem from input-dependent conditioning rather than additional learnable weights, and the approach is most useful when recurring local motifs change relevance across sequence-level contexts.

## [Quantum Recurrent Models Show No Advantage in Financial Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15298) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.15298) evaluates quantum-classical hybrid recurrent architectures—a Quantum LSTM (QLSTM) and Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC)—against classical baselines for financial time-series forecasting. Using a synthetic monthly revenue series of 1056 months, ten seeds, and multiple benchmarks, the study finds no evidence of quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage in this low-dimensional setting. This rigorous negative result is important for the quantum machine learning community, as it challenges claims that quantum circuits inherently provide parameter efficiency or accuracy gains for time-series tasks. It suggests that reported advantages may stem from architectural choices rather than quantum effects, urging more careful controlled comparisons. The QLSTM with 2,105 parameters was statistically indistinguishable from an LSTM 126 times larger, but also indistinguishable from a matched classical control and a plain LSTM of the same budget, so its efficiency cannot be attributed to quantum circuits. The quantum reservoir underperformed a classical reservoir of equal feature dimension in all ten seeds and was worse than SARIMA, while all recurrent models and classical reservoirs improved on SARIMA by about 2% in RMSE.

## [ReShap: Interpretable RL for High-Dimensional Multi-Action Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15507) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ReShap is a policy-distillation framework that extends Shapley-based interpretability to high-dimensional, multi-action reinforcement learning environments by extracting compact features from raw image observations, performing SHAP-based feature attribution, and distilling deep RL policies into interpretable surrogates (decision trees, linear regression, logistic regression). Evaluated on Atari and Box2D with three deep RL algorithms, it preserves competitive task performance, with decision trees generally outperforming linear and logistic regression. This work addresses a key limitation of prior Shapley-based interpretability methods like SILVER, which were restricted to low-dimensional state spaces and binary actions, making them impractical for real-world vision-based control tasks. By enabling interpretability in high-dimensional, multi-action settings, ReShap could improve trust and adoption of deep RL in safety-critical domains such as robotics and autonomous systems. ReShap distills the policy using the full set of (state, policy-action) pairs along the policy's visited distribution, and a human-subject study was conducted to assess clarity and trustworthiness. Decision trees generally outperform linear and logistic regression surrogates, while linear regression is weakest in most settings.

A new arXiv paper (2611.15523) constructs a finite-world learning setup in which a neural network learns care as a child and then tests whether that care survives the mother's departure, new situations, and further learning. The mechanism combines a vocabulary of harm, a learned measure of future acceptability, an execution veto, and certified updates that preserve the care boundary. This work offers a formal, testable interpretation of Geoffrey Hinton's high-profile suggestion that AI should be given maternal instincts, moving the debate from metaphor toward explicit conditions on representation, supervision, and execution. If such conditions can be validated, they could inform safety architectures that remain robust as models continue to learn after deployment. The paper proves preservation under repeated accepted updates and gives a necessary and sufficient condition for readout feasibility, supported by a water-and-speech experiment where protected networks complete 270 speech episodes without a harmful word and incur no avoidable harm across 486 episodes. It also presents two-request and finite-stock counterexamples identifying when the role code ceases to suffice, and shows that removing future lookahead permits avoidable lapses.

GLOBAFED introduces a probabilistic neural network surrogate with a shared feature-extracting backbone and agent-specific variational Bayesian last layers to enable efficient knowledge transfer in federated Bayesian optimization across heterogeneous objectives without compromising privacy. This work relaxes restrictive assumptions of prior federated Bayesian optimization methods, such as near-identical objectives or shared Gaussian process hyperparameters, making federated optimization more practical for real-world heterogeneous settings. Agents collaboratively train the shared backbone via federated learning to build a common latent representation while keeping agent-specific heads local, and the variational Bayesian last layers provide uncertainty estimates for Bayesian optimization; experiments show faster convergence and better final performance than state-of-the-art FedBO baselines.

## [PriorSplit keeps step-order priors outside VLM agents to handle missing frames](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15766) ⭐️ 6.0/10

PriorSplit is a training-free method that stores step-order priors outside a vision-language model trained with on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), using counts of which neighboring step comes first to fill in missing frames at deployment. Experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in web, cooking, and egocentric tasks show it outperforms all compared methods when frames are missing, at the same training cost as OPSD. This addresses a key failure mode in self-evolving VLM agents where internalized memory can override perception when frames are missing or reordered, which is common in real-world deployment. The approach offers a simple, training-free fix that could improve robustness of agents that learn skills from visual demonstrations. PriorSplit counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes; at inference, the model checks if both asked steps are in view and answers from frames if so, otherwise from the counts. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills, it stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that store order fall behind.

## [ADAPT: Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing for Pull Requests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16114) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ADAPT introduces an autonomous coding agent that generates change-focused regression tests for pull requests by analyzing the diff between base and head versions, planning and generating candidate unit tests, and iteratively refining them using a fail-to-pass (F2P) verification tool that checks which changed lines remain uncovered. Evaluated on 426 real-world PRs, ADAPT+GPT-4o achieves a 62.0% F2P rate (264/426) versus BLAST's 35.4% (151/426), while ADAPT+GPT-5-mini reaches 89.9% (383/426). This work addresses a critical gap in PR testing: developers often omit tests for new behavior, leaving changes unguarded against future regressions. By focusing on the specific behavior introduced by a change rather than overall code coverage, ADAPT could significantly improve regression safety and reduce manual test-writing effort in modern CI/CD workflows. ADAPT uses a dedicated F2P verification tool that runs each candidate test on both base and head versions, and after F2P success, reports uncovered changed lines to guide iterative refinement. On 137 PRs shared with Change And Cover (ChaCo), ADAPT achieves full patch coverage on 83.9% of PRs versus 79.6% for ChaCo, at considerably lower time and cost, and manual evaluation shows mean scores up to 4.54/5 for importance, 4.35/5 for assertion strength, and 4.49/5 for readability.

A new arXiv paper (2611.16182) argues that the JEPA proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) is vacuous under same-state positive pairs with hard-whitening, because the induced world kernel becomes the identity and uniqueness fails. Only one of the paper's four quantitative results survives: a gap-free lower bound that vanishes only at perfect scene-explained fraction. This critique challenges a theoretical foundation linking JEPA architectures to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, suggesting that the uniqueness claim for learned representations may be conditional and not generally valid. It matters for researchers in representation learning theory who rely on such proofs to justify convergence properties of self-supervised models. Under the hard-whitening population objective, every centered whitened state function is a global minimizer, and when d_z-1 ≥ 2k, two minimizers can have best-rotation squared residual 2k. The uniqueness claim is conditional; for k < d_z-1 its idealized same-state limit is vacuous, and a canonical frame is determined only up to a rotation and a latent permutation.

## [SUMNO: Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16341) ⭐️ 6.0/10

SUMNO introduces a spatially unrolled multigrid neural operator that maps a V-cycle into a feed-forward U-shaped network for fluid flow surrogate modeling, using parameter-free down- and upsampling for restriction and prolongation, and additive skip connections for coarse-grid correction. Evaluated on four unsteady and steady flow benchmarks against five baselines, it is best in 5 of 7 settings and reduces 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% relative to the strongest baseline, while outperforming three baselines with over 130 million parameters using only 9.4 million parameters. This work bridges classical geometric multigrid concepts with modern neural operator design, offering a more physically grounded architecture for accelerating computational fluid dynamics surrogates. Its strong accuracy with a small parameter budget suggests that multigrid-inspired inductive biases can improve efficiency and generalization in scientific machine learning for flow prediction. The architecture uses convolutions at fine and intermediate resolutions and shifted-window attention at the coarsest level, with window partitioning generalized to handle periodicity independently per axis, and normalization-free transfer and skip pathways. It is limited to regular grids and evaluated on a set of benchmark flows, so generalization to complex geometries and unstructured meshes remains to be shown.

**Background**: Neural operators, such as Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) and DeepONet, learn mappings between function spaces to serve as fast surrogate models for solving partial differential equations, including CFD simulations. Geometric multigrid (GMG) is a classical numerical method that solves PDEs on a hierarchy of grids using restriction (downsampling) and prolongation (upsampling) operators in a V-cycle to efficiently reduce errors across scales. U-shaped networks like U-Net resemble this multi-resolution structure and have become popular in surrogate modeling, but their components often follow generic vision practices rather than multigrid principles.

## [DRAMA: Training-Free Acceleration for Multimodal Diffusion LLMs via Attention Redundancy Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16345) ⭐️ 6.0/10

DRAMA introduces a training-free acceleration framework for multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) that systematically dissects attention redundancy along spatial and temporal axes, revealing two persistent structures: attention mass concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms—Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS)—which together achieve an average 18.67× inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification, or attention caching. Multimodal dLLMs offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive vision-language models but suffer from high inference cost due to full forward passes over long multimodal sequences at each denoising step. DRAMA's measurement-grounded approach provides a strong acceleration baseline that could make dLLMs more practical for real-world deployment, potentially influencing future efficient inference designs in the diffusion LLM ecosystem. The speedup is achieved without training, architectural changes, or attention caching, relying solely on pruning redundant visual tokens and adaptively stopping denoising when sufficient. The framework maintains competitive accuracy across six benchmarks, though the abstract does not specify the exact accuracy trade-off or the models tested.

## [HyBridge: Bridge-Guided Hyperbolic Hypergraph Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16351) ⭐️ 6.0/10

HyBridge is a new self-supervised hyperbolic hypergraph representation learning framework that estimates node bridge scores from the external connectivity of individual hyperedges, then guides node radial positions in hyperbolic space accordingly. Experiments on 10 real-world hypergraphs show it outperforms 22 competing methods, with up to 9.82% improvement in node classification. This work addresses why simply porting hypergraph representation learning to hyperbolic space does not consistently help, by linking node structural roles to embedding radii. It offers a principled way to better model tree-like groupwise structures, which could benefit domains such as social networks, bioinformatics, and recommendation systems that rely on hypergraph-based relational learning. The method combines hyperedge-aware bridge score estimation, hyperbolic hypergraph encoding of node and hyperedge embeddings, radial position guidance by bridge scores, and contrastive learning to preserve node discriminability. The authors note that the conventional graph-based relationship between bridge nodes and centrality does not consistently hold in hypergraphs, motivating their hyperedge-level estimation; code is released anonymously for reproducibility.

SoScale introduces a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization that optimizes layer-output fidelity via a Hessian-aware objective coupled with GPTQ-style error recovery. Across Qwen3 models, it consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 formats. Accurate FP4 quantization is critical for reducing LLM memory footprint and inference cost, and SoScale's layer-output-aware scale search offers a practical improvement over existing element-wise methods. This could benefit deployment of large models on hardware supporting FP4 formats like MXFP4 and NVFP4. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs rather than local reconstruction error. It couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, and experiments show consistent gains across Qwen3 models under three FP4 formats.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory and compute requirements of LLMs by representing weights in fewer bits. FP4 formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 use 4-bit floating-point payloads with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy sensitive to scaling choices. Default max-absolute-value scaling can waste FP4 levels on outliers, and existing scale-search methods optimize tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. Hessian-aware methods like HAWQ use second-order information to guide quantization, and GPTQ-style error recovery compensates for quantization errors block-wise.

PISim is a unified photonic inference simulator that couples pretrained DNN execution with physics-based models of six accelerator architectures, six electro-optic modulators, four optical source organizations, and direct or coherent readout schemes. It embeds stage-resolved impairment operators and an analytical cycle-level timing model to enable hardware-aware cross-layer design-space exploration. ## [Silent Neuron Theory Preserves Plasticity for Adaptive Video Streaming RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01584) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces the Silent Neuron theory, a new framework that better characterizes neural plasticity loss than existing dormant neuron metrics, and proposes Reset Silent Neuron (ReSiN), a method that strategically resets neurons based on forward and backward propagation states. In an adaptive video streaming system, ReSiN improves QoE by 178% under non-stationary bandwidth conditions and by 1.6% under stationary real-world traces. This work addresses a critical but often overlooked problem in deep reinforcement learning—plasticity loss—which hinders agents' ability to adapt to changing environments, and demonstrates its practical impact in adaptive video streaming where network conditions are highly variable. The theoretical framework and the ReSiN method could be generalized to other RL applications requiring continual adaptation. ReSiN guides neuron resets using both forward and backward propagation states, and the paper establishes a tighter performance bound for ReSiN under non-stationary network conditions. The code will be available at https://tinyzqh.github.io/ReSiN/.

Researchers introduce Normalized Base-2 Encoding (NB2E), an input encoding that enables vanilla multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to extrapolate four periodic waveforms without prior knowledge of their functional form. The method confines intervention to early denoising steps via a piecewise guidance schedule, and the Laplacian sharpening principle generalizes beyond motion to steer complex non-linear concepts such as precise object numerosity. ## [DHRL uses MDP homomorphisms to tackle delayed feedback in RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03641) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes delayed homomorphic reinforcement learning (DHRL), a framework that introduces a belief-equivalence relation over the augmented state space to collapse control-redundant augmented states into a compact abstract state space. For continuous domains, it introduces deep delayed homomorphic policy gradient (D²HPG), which outperforms strong augmentation-based baselines on MuJoCo benchmarks, especially in long-delay regimes. Delayed feedback is common in real-world systems and breaks the Markov assumption, and existing augmentation-based methods suffer from state-space explosion. DHRL provides a unified abstraction mechanism that benefits both actor and critic, potentially improving sample efficiency and performance in delayed-reward settings. The framework yields exact abstraction under deterministic dynamics and approximate abstraction under stochastic dynamics; in finite domains, exact abstraction preserves optimality and recovers the delay-free sample-complexity order, while approximate abstraction admits a bound on value loss. Code is available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning typically assumes the Markov property, meaning the current state fully captures the relevant information for decision-making. Delayed feedback violates this assumption, and a common remedy is to augment the state with action histories, but this leads to exponential growth in state space. MDP homomorphisms are mappings that preserve the structure of Markov decision processes, enabling state abstraction by grouping equivalent states.

## [COSAC: Critic-Free Counterfactual Credit Assignment for Sequential Cooperative Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17693) ⭐️ 6.0/10

COSAC introduces a critic-free policy gradient framework that assigns per-agent credit in sequential cooperative teams by fitting an additive reward decomposition via a single ridge regression on the rollout batch, and computes counterfactual advantages from fictitious policy continuations without extra environment or reward calls. The method instantiates the Sequential Aristocrat Utility (SeqAU), with bias and variance bounds derived, and in sequential multi-agent LLM fine-tuning it reduces training regret by 17% on consensus-based science reasoning versus the best critic-free baseline and by 61% on Python coding versus MA-GRPO. Credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent systems is a core bottleneck, especially as team size grows, and critic-based methods scale poorly due to costly joint or factored critics. COSAC's critic-free approach avoids this scaling issue and shows concrete gains in multi-agent LLM fine-tuning, suggesting a practical path for training teams of language models and sequential robotic agents. The theoretical analysis shows that the direct-effect bias bound has no explicit team-size factor, while the indirect effect's reward-noise bound scales with the number of downstream agents; experiments include sequential bandits up to K=16 and multi-agent LLM fine-tuning. The approach replaces importance-sampling reweighting and per-agent environment replay with policy forward passes, but relies on a linear additive decomposition that may limit expressiveness in highly non-additive reward settings.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, a team of agents shares a single team-level reward, making it difficult to determine how much each agent contributed—a problem known as credit assignment. Traditional actor-critic methods use a centralized critic to estimate individual contributions, but maintaining a joint critic becomes expensive as the number of agents grows. Critic-free alternatives exist but suffer from issues like coupled noise across agents, high-variance importance-sampling corrections, or costly per-agent counterfactual replays. COSAC addresses these by using ridge regression to decompose the team reward and by generating counterfactual advantages through fictitious policy continuations.

## [Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference Improves Semisupervised Mean Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21260) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference, a post-hoc calibration method that calibrates prediction scores on labeled data before semisupervised mean estimation. It provides theoretical guarantees for isotonic calibration and shows linear calibration is first-order equivalent to PPI++. This work bridges prediction-powered inference and semisupervised inference by showing how calibration can improve efficiency when prediction models are miscalibrated, potentially leading to more reliable estimates in fields that rely on large unlabeled datasets with small labeled samples. For isotonic calibration, the authors establish first-order optimality: post-processing can improve predictive accuracy and estimator efficiency, and replacing the fitted isotonic score with its conditional-mean oracle yields no additional first-order variance reduction. They also clarify that the original PPI estimator is a special case of AIPW and can be inefficient when the prediction model is accurate, while PPI++ is AIPW with empirical efficiency maximization.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Prediction-powered inference (PPI) is a framework for valid statistical inference when a small labeled dataset is supplemented with predictions from a machine-learning model on a larger unlabeled dataset. Augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) is a doubly robust estimator that combines outcome regression and inverse probability weighting, protecting against model misspecification. Calibration adjusts prediction scores to better align with true outcomes, and isotonic calibration is a non-parametric method that fits a monotonic function to map scores to probabilities.

The paper introduces variable-size supervertex (vSV) partitioning, which groups cortical surface vertices into patches analogous to superpixels, and designs a Vision Transformer (vSV-ViT) that processes these vSVs via padding, mask-aware patch embedding, and vertex position embedding. Fast-dLLM++ introduces Fréchet profile decoding, a training-free method that selects parallel commit sets from the full sorted confidence profile rather than a single worst-case confidence, generalizing Fast-dLLM's factor selector. It recovers the previous rule exactly in the equal-confidence case and adds a provable heterogeneity bonus when selected tokens have uneven confidences.

It decomposes endpoint recovery into an image-like anchor and a noise-oriented residual, avoiding iterative inversion and repeated evaluation of a diffusion-scale U-Net. A new arXiv paper (2610.11963v2) proposes an execution-based pipeline that uses computer-use agents to automatically verify whether LLM-generated no-code fixes actually resolve bug reports in a real browser environment. This work addresses a practical gap in software engineering: no-code fixes (e.g., directing users to change settings or update versions) are time-consuming to verify manually, and LLMs are increasingly used to generate them. Only 17.6% of candidate issues could be set up and pass both sanity gates, and the three executors (OpenCUA-72B, Claude Sonnet 5, and Meta's Muse Glimmer) reached the same verdict on only 46.9% of fixes. Compared with human execution, executors matched human consensus for 66.1% to 88.1% of sampled fixes, and even under the best executor fewer than half of LLM-generated no-code fixes resolved the reported bug.

## [Conformal Factuality Filtering Evaluated in Agentic RAG Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34872) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper formalizes agent-driven adaptive retrieval and evaluates post-generation conformal claim filtering using GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B across HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA. Experiments show that stricter conformal targets consistently increase response-level factual support but reduce claim retention and non-empty response coverage. This work provides an empirical foundation for applying conformal prediction to improve factual reliability in agentic RAG, highlighting the trade-off between factual support and answer availability. It informs the design of more trustworthy retrieval-augmented systems that autonomously decide when to retrieve. The study characterizes a query-aware relevance-scoring formulation that accounts for evidence collected across successive retrieval decisions, and the trade-offs vary across models and datasets, underscoring the need to jointly evaluate factual reliability and answer availability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances language model responses by incorporating external evidence, but retrieved information alone does not guarantee factual support for generated claims. Agentic RAG extends this by letting an agent iteratively decide whether to retrieve more information or stop, complicating evidence acquisition. Conformal prediction is a statistical framework that provides uncertainty guarantees by filtering claims that fail a calibrated threshold, and prior work has applied it to LLM factuality but not in adaptive retrieval settings.

## [CGSE Uses Critic-Guided Actions in Latent World Models to Augment Offline RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39100) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE), which augments an offline dataset by sampling candidate actions from an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order Q-function approximation within a trust region. A frozen latent world model then imagines the next state for each refined action, and the critic selects the best transition to append to the replay buffer. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative 7.1% on average success rate. This work offers a way to generate additional training experience offline without costly or unsafe real-world interaction, potentially improving the scalability of offline reinforcement learning. It is most relevant to researchers working on model-based offline RL and data augmentation for control tasks. CGSE requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as synthetic experience is generated entirely offline using the frozen world model. The method keeps the offline critic fixed while training the actor on the synthetic transitions, and actions are selected via short-horizon search with single model steps.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn policies from fixed datasets without online interaction, but performance is often limited by dataset coverage. World models learn a compressed latent representation of environment dynamics, allowing agents to 'imagine' rollouts, yet compounding errors in long imagined rollouts can degrade policy learning. Trust regions constrain policy or action updates to stay close to the data distribution, mitigating extrapolation errors in offline RL.

## [Hybrid Retrieval, NLI, and Open-Source LLMs Tested for Scientific Claim Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03093) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.03093v2) experimentally evaluates a conservative fusion rule that combines hybrid retrieval, NLI models, and open-source LLMs for scientific claim verification, using a newly constructed benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact. The study finds that Qwen3 8B achieves the highest Macro-F1 (0.7937), while the NLI baseline (DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli) reaches only 0.3157, and contrary to the hypothesis, fusing NLI with LLMs degrades performance. This work provides a useful incremental contribution by quantifying the strengths and weaknesses of NLI versus LLM-based verifiers and showing that a simple conservative fusion can hurt rather than help, which cautions against naive ensemble approaches in claim verification pipelines. It also releases a sizable benchmark that could support future research on evidence-based scientific fact-checking. The benchmark contains 858 Support, 152 Contradict, and 1,025 Not Enough Evidence claims, with the top five sentences per claim retrieved via a hybrid of semantic and BM25 lexical retrieval that slightly outperforms either method alone. Fusion drops Macro-F1 to 0.7392 for Qwen3, 0.6730 for Llama 3.1, and 0.5991 for Mistral, and error analysis shows that NLI-LLM disagreements often overturn correct LLM predictions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Claim verification is the task of deciding whether a source text supports, contradicts, or lacks sufficient evidence for a claim. Natural Language Inference (NLI) models classify pairs of sentences as entailment, contradiction, or neutral, but struggle when evidence spans multiple sentences, whereas Large Language Models (LLMs) can reason across sentences but may hallucinate unsupported conclusions. SciFact and CliniFact are benchmarks for scientific and clinical claim verification, and hybrid retrieval combines BM25 lexical matching with dense semantic search to find relevant evidence.

## [Label-Wording Augmentation Helps Unfamiliar Words, Not Abbreviations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08439) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper compares two releases of Ru-Jev, a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks, where the later release adds label-wording augmentation that presents labels in multiple surface forms. Testing ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates, the augmented model shows higher point accuracy on held-out vocabularies of ordinary or borrowed words (by up to 0.24) but no usable gain on abbreviations or opaque codes. This work highlights a practical robustness issue for typed-decision models, whose accuracy depends on label wording supplied at request time and not controlled by the developer. The finding that augmentation helps with unfamiliar words but not abbreviations or codes can guide practitioners in designing more reliable label-scoring systems. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation, and the earlier recipe varies across seeds by up to 0.098 on the strictest slice. Several gains rest partly on one label that the earlier release almost never chose; fitting one bias per option removes part of them, while the jargon gain largely survives. On two unseen datasets, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points, narrowed to -3.4 and +1.4 after per-option bias correction.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: A cross-encoder is a neural architecture that processes a pair of inputs jointly through a single model to produce a relevance or classification score. Typed-decision models score options supplied by the caller at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model developer does not control. Label-wording augmentation is a data augmentation technique that presents labels in multiple surface forms during training to improve robustness to wording variations.

## [Jev Decision Models Benchmarked Against 20 LLMs on 43 Arabic Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10802) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper evaluates 67 systems—47 decision models including Jev 1.14.0 and Jev 1.13.0, plus 20 large language models—on 43 Arabic tasks across 9 task families under a shared zero-shot protocol. Jev 1.14.0 scored 69.24 (on a 100-point scale) versus 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0, while Gemma-4-31B led the aggregate at 71.81. This is one of the first broad, systematic comparisons of decision models like Jev against mainstream LLMs on Arabic NLP, covering both Modern Standard Arabic and dialects. It highlights that aggregate scores can mask large task-family and dialect-specific variation, which matters for anyone deploying models in Arabic-speaking markets. The suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, and removing these controls, repeated cross-task items, or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps for Jev 1.14.0 range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets, and a Palestinian banking penalty is larger for Jev 1.14.0 than for Gemma-4-31B or Jais-2-8B.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) is the standardized literary variety used across the Arab world, while spoken dialects differ substantially by region and can be much harder for NLP systems. Zero-shot evaluation means models are tested on tasks without any task-specific training examples. Jev is a family of decision models positioned for automation and software tasks, and this paper tests how it fares against LLMs on Arabic.

## [Failure traces yield modest 4-point gain in agent harness notes, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11342) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.11342v2) empirically evaluates whether an AI agent's harness notes can learn from its failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. Using a frozen 9-billion-parameter model with notes written by a larger teacher model, the authors find that failure-based notes improve accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over a matched search baseline on generated customer-service decisions, but about 60% of that gain comes from the search process itself, and no improvement appears in full conversations. This is a useful, honest negative-ish result for the agent self-improvement literature: it suggests that much of the apparent benefit from failure traces may be attributable to the optimization process rather than the traces themselves, cautioning against over-claiming gains from learning on failures. It affects researchers and practitioners building agent harnesses that aim to improve without retraining model weights. The study is limited to a single 9B model and customer-service tasks, and the abstract is truncated, reducing clarity. A strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons (still awaiting tests on new data) and one tool-use lesson that showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks; a neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory), and a blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: In agent self-improvement with frozen weights, the model's parameters are not updated; instead, the agent's "harness"—the notes, prompts, or procedures around the model—is optimized. Failure traces are records of the agent's mistakes, which researchers hope can inform better harness notes. A matched search baseline is a control condition that runs the same note-optimization process but with the failure traces withheld, isolating the added value of the traces themselves.

## [TRACE-based AI assistant screens draft laws for corruption risks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14244) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents an AI assistant built on the TRACE architecture that automates anti-corruption expertise of draft legislation by flagging provisions an expert would criticize and naming the regulatory defect. The system was evaluated on an open benchmark of 132 Ukrainian draft laws with 474 findings from NAZK conclusions, achieving recall of 0.28–0.46 on top-ten flags depending on the model used. This work demonstrates a practical application of LLMs to a socially important but niche domain—anti-corruption legal review—and provides an open benchmark constructed from real government findings. It could inform future efforts to assist under-resourced oversight bodies, though modest recall and the lack of human expert validation limit immediate deployment. The pipeline combines deterministic parsing, model-guided single-provision qualification, rule-based factor assignment, and human oversight. Most misses occur on provisions the system located but qualified as a different risk, and none of the 32 legal-collision findings were matched; scores reflect agreement with model-extracted findings rated by an LLM judge without human expert validation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 14, 05:00

**Background**: TRACE is an architecture for structuring AI-assisted legal analysis, though the paper assumes familiarity with its components. Ukraine's National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAZK) is one of the country's four anti-corruption pillars, created after the Euromaidan revolution, and publishes conclusions on draft laws that serve as ground truth here. LLM-as-a-judge is an increasingly used evaluation method in legal NLP, but its reliability remains debated.
